speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. On page 5892 of Hansard during the discussion of the bill of rights on July 7, 1960, I am reported as having said:
(Translation):
Where was his former leader, the leader of the opposition, Hon. Mr. Drew, who is now in London? Where was he at that time?
(Text):
It is evident that the word "lui" refers to Mr. Drew and not to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. On page 3 of the translation there appears the following:
Where was his former chief, the leader of the opposition, the Hon. Mr. Drew, who is now in London? Where was he, himself, at that time?
The translation by the use of the word "himself" for the word "lui" refers to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi. To say the least the translation, while not inaccur-rate, is ambiguous. I had no one else in mind at the time but Mr. Drew.
This, sir, later led to an intervention by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Morris), who made a number of affirmations that are not in accordance with the record, who referred to the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi and who also left a clear inference that Hansard had been changed. I raise this as a question of privilege because the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made exactly the same charge against the Prime Minister during the course of the same debate, and realizing that he had spoken hastily immediately arose and asked that the words be withdrawn. Under the circumstances I trust that the hon. member for Halifax will do likewise.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: The hon. member, of course, is free to do as he wishes. The point ought to have been taken at the time the incident arose. It would be extremely difficult to pursue matters of privilege after they have passed into the record.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext:
Still on the question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, if you will allow me to do so I should like to say this. I was not
in the house when the words complained of were uttered. I came in toward the end of the speech of the hon. member. I have been absent from the house in the last two days. Therefore I could not raise the matter any sooner than at this moment.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: On the same question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out that I raised the matter at the time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: If the hon. member feels that it is a matter which he had not an opportunity to raise earlier and that he would like to raise now, I feel that he ought to be more explicit in order to make a prima facie case of privilege. The inference that the record would be changed, unless it is attached to some hon. member specifically, while it might be offensive to the house is not something for an individual to complain of.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: I am not going to press the matter unduly, but the words used by the hon. member for Halifax were these: "Well, unless the Hansard record is changed we shall all be able to see the truth." The words used by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate were practically the same.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: They were the same. The hon. member is correct about that matter. Unless the inference is associated directly with an hon. member-

maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: It was.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: -in order to give the implication that he is one who would change the record-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: That is what it does. It is associated directly with my intention to change the record. I say now that I did not change the record, nor did I alter it. All I am saying is that under the circumstances it would seem to me that if the hon. member for Halifax followed the same procedure as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, he should act accordingly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVILEGE
subtopic: MR. CHEVRIER  CLARIFICATION OF TRANSLATION -ALLEGED CHANGING OF RECORD
speechtext: The hon. member is at liberty to comment on the point if he wishes to do so.

subtopic: APPOINTMENTS OF DEPUTY MINISTER OF WELFARE AND QUEEN'S PRINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two appointments that I wish to announce.
The first is that the government has appointed Dr. J. W. Willard as deputy minister of welfare in the Department of National Health and Welfare. He has been director of research in the department for the past 13 years, originally entering the public service in April of 1941 with the unemployment insurance commission. He transferred to the Department of National Defence at the beginning of 1943 and served as an administrative officer with the Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps during the war, attaining the rank of major. In the spring of 1945 he was appointed executive secretary of the Canadian medical procurement and assignment board, which position he held until he was appointed to the Department of National Health and Welfare.
Then there is the appointment of the Queen's printer. The governor in council has appointed Mr. Roger Duhamel who is already well known to many hon. members of the house. It might be recalled that he has had a distinguished career in journalism and publishing. Trained as a lawyer, he was employed for a time with the city of Montreal but soon became assistant chief editor of Le Canada. Subsequently, he held editorial positions with Le Devoir and La Patrie, then became director of the Montreal Matin. He was chief editor of La Patrie until his appointment in 1958 to the board of broadcast governors, from which he is resigning.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN FREEDOM FROM HUNGER CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. In view of the recent announcement of the director general of the
Inquiries of the Ministry food and agriculture organization to the effect that a five-year freedom from hunger campaign has been launched by the United Nations organization, can the minister inform the house whether Canada will co-operate in the implementation of the main features of this program? More particularly, will Canada provide technical assistance, and will some of our surplus food be made available?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN FREEDOM FROM HUNGER CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the answer to this question will be a little longer than you usually like, but I shall be glad to give it.
The freedom from hunger campaign of the food and agriculture organization is designed primarily to stimulate the provision of technical assistance to food deficient countries, and to interest and encourage the participation of non-government bodies and private individuals in the work of FAO. The program does not envisage the supplying of food from surplus countries to deficiency countries. Rather it is designed to broaden and accelerate the technical assistance activities of FAO to enable deficiency countries to expand their own food production.
At the tenth conference of FAO in Rome in 1959, Canada supported the proposal for the freedom from hunger campaign, although pointing out that in addition to its contribution to FAO Canada was contributing a large amount of technical assistance under the Colombo plan and similar plans for Nigeria, Ghana and the West Indies federation. In addition we are now providing training facilities in Canada on seed improvement for a second group from several eastern countries in connection with the world seed improvement campaign, which is now part of the freedom from hunger campaign.
On May 30 there was an informal meeting of representatives of some 20 non-governmental organizations in Ottawa to plan for the establishment of a continuing Canadian committee for the freedom from hunger campaign. This group and others who have expressed an interest will meet with Dr. B. R. Sen, director general of FAO in Ottawa on August 18 to lay more formal plans for Canadian participation.

maintopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN FREEDOM FROM HUNGER CAMPAIGN
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Could the minister give the house some idea what amount of money Canada will make available under this program?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: CANADIAN PARTICIPATION IN FREEDOM FROM HUNGER CAMPAIGN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, until the meeting with Dr. Sen has been held in August there are no firm plans or commitments in connection with the campaign.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, July 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Churchill:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the ratification by Canada of the protocol, signed at Moscow, on April 18, 1960, renewing the agreement on trade between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, concluded in Ottawa, on February 29, 1956, and that this house do approve the same.
Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce: Mr. Speaker, on April 25 of this year I announced the signing of a protocol renewing the trade agreement of 1956 between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. I stated at that time that an opportunity would be provided for a debate on this protocol in advance of its ratification.
The protocol renews for a further three years the 1956 agreement, with the exception of article IX, and the letters which the two parties exchanged at that time concerning the right of the Canadian government to fix under the Canadian Customs Act values of goods for ordinary and special duty. The house approved ratification of this agreement on April 18, 1956, and the other place gave its approval on April 26 of that year.
Article IX of the 1956 agreement, which is not renewed, provided for signature and ratification at that time. It also stipulated that negotiations may be held to renew the agreement. These negotiations were success-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
fully completed with the signing of the protocol in Moscow on April 18 of this year.
The main features of the agreement may be outlined as follows. Provision is made in it for the exchange of most favoured nation treatment between the two governments, and the term "most favoured nation treatment" refers to tariffs and related matters in the field of commerce. It has the effect of placing Canadian commercial relations with the U.S.S.R. on a basis similar to our relations with most other countries. Most favoured nation treatment does not involve the extension of the British preferential rates of duty to imports from the U.S.S.R. Article VII specifically provides that most favoured nation treatment shall not apply to exclusive advantages accorded by Canada to members of the British commonwealth of nations and the republic of Ireland.
When I announced the signing of the protocol I made it clear that it would not affect our strategic export controls. A provision is included in the agreement which permits either government to apply prohibitions or restrictions of any kind for the protection of its essential security interests.
Another clause which I outlined refers to the treatment of merchant ships of either country in the seaports of the other, assuring them of as favourable treatment as the merchant vessels of other countries. This simply confirms the situation which existed previously with regard to ships of U.S.S.R. registry. The provision does not apply to the performance of harbour services or to coastal shipping.
There are also provisions which refer to the legal status of persons, access to courts and arbitration. These clauses do not establish any new procedure for settling disputes arising in the conduct of trade between Canada and the U.S.S.R. They merely indicate the facilities available if such disputes should arise. Canadians are free to choose between Canadian or Soviet courts, and they are not bound to enter arbitration.
From the Canadian point of view the most important part of the renewed agreement is an exchange of letters between myself and the minister of foreign trade of U.S.S.R., Mr. N. S. Patolichev. The letters provide that in each year of the renewed agreement the Soviet foreign trade organization will purchase Canadian goods to a value of $25 million, including not less than 200,000 metric tons of Canadian wheat, which in bushels is approximately 7.5 million, provided the total annual value of Canadian purchases from the U.S.S.R. is not less than $12.5 million. Should the total value of Canadian purchases from the U.S.S.R. be less than $12.5 million in any one year, the Soviet undertaking to

purchase from Canada would be reduced and would be determined on a two to one basis; that is, the Soviet union would purchase twice as much from Canada as Canada imported from the Soviet union. Wheat will constitute not less than half the amount of such annual Soviet purchases.
It will be noted that Canada does not give any undertaking in this agreement to purchase from the U.S.S.R. The major commitment made by Canada is to allow imports from the Soviet union to compete on equal terms with imports from other countries receiving most favoured nation treatment.
The letters also provide that the authorities of the two countries will consult periodically concerning the implementation of the agreement and any other matters affecting trade relations between the two countries. Under the earlier agreement the consultation provision and the undertaking of both parties to give sympathetic consideration to each other's representations were limited to matters concerning the implementation of the agreement. The broadening of these to include other matters affecting trade relations would permit Canada, for example, to take up with the Soviet government problems arising out of Soviet selling practices in world markets that may be unfair and harmful to our export interests. Consultations will take place annually, and should permit the development of closer co-operation and understanding with the Soviet authorities concerned with trade.
To conclude the description of the arrangements to be ratified by the government, I might mention that the protocol will terminate three years from the date of signature and consequently a further renewal, if it should then be desired, would be a matter for negotiation.
As I stated earlier, 200,000 tons of wheat will be purchased annually from Canada under the terms of the new agreement if our annual imports reach a value of $12.5 million. In the previous agreement the total Soviet purchase commitment was for 400,000 tons of wheat a year. It will be appreciated that the situation has changed markedly since 1956. The Soviet union has greatly enlarged its production of wheat and is now a regular exporter. Moreover, the level of sales achieved by the Russians under the previous agreement did not come up to expectations, and they were not prepared to continue trading on the previous basis. In addition, since 1956 the Soviet union has concluded a number of trade agreements with non-communist countries in which they have avoided making unilateral and unconditional purchase commitments.
79951-0-385J
Trade Agreement with Russia
As a result of these new conditions they were not willing to renew the previous purchase commitment without modifications. However, the arrangements that have been made for trade on a two to one ratio do involve a purchase commitment on the Soviet side, and the terms of the arrangement are better than those offered by the U.S.S.R. to any other country. Provided the businessmen and traders of the two countries take advantage of the sales opportunities which exist, we may expect that under the new agreement substantial quantities of Canadian commodities, including wheat, will again be sold.
I am sure the house is aware of the vast differences between the methods of conducting foreign trade in this country and in the Soviet union. In Canada most trade is in private hands, and decisions to purchase and sell goods abroad are made by private persons. Against this, Soviet foreign trade transactions are made within the framework of government policy by officials of monopolistic state trading organizations. A variety of problems result from these differences in the way of doing business.
A characteristic of the Soviet state trading system is a strong inclination toward bilateral arrangements, including barter transactions. Many of their trade agreements involve mutual undertakings to purchase specified amounts of listed goods. In other cases, targets for the exchange of goods are established which the Soviet authorities are able to implement as regards their foreign purchases through control over imports. With regard to exports, different but related considerations apply. The experience of the Soviet union in selling in open competitive markets, such as that of Canada, is relatively limited by comparison with many of our trading partners whose sales are promoted by private businessmen. On the Canadian side, our exporters have in general had little experience in dealing with the complex state trading organizations which have responsibility for executing the import programs of the Soviet union.
The new arrangements provide a favourable framework for the traders and trading organizations of the two countries to establish and expand their business relationships. The success of the agreement from the standpoint of Canada's trade will hinge upon the results achieved by the Canadian business community in its dealing with Soviet trading corporations. Canadian exporters interested in sales to the U.S.S.R. will need to find out how best to develop the Soviet market, both from the point of view of the products to be sold and the ways and means

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Trade Agreement with Russia of encouraging the Soviet import organizations to buy. For their part the Soviet export organizations, if they wish to expand their sales in Canada, will have to make the necessary effort to ascertain what Soviet products may be saleable in the Canadian market and how these sales can be developed on an orderly basis.
Several steps have been taken to promote the development of trade between our two countries. Canadian businessmen may have an opportunity to discuss their trade interests with a Soviet trade mission which may come to Canada later this year. Soviet authorities informed me that they would welcome a comparable visit of Canadian businessmen to the Soviet union. As a service to the business community interested in trade with the U.S.S.R., a commercial counsellor has been assigned to the Canadian embassy in Moscow. Numerous firms are already exploring the Soviet market with his assistance. For their part, the Soviet union have expressed an interest in stepping up their efforts to develop sales in the Canadian market. The conditions for trade have been established and a spirit of good will and co-operation in the commercial field has been initiated. It is the hope of the government that the envisaged levels of trade will be realized and that we may look forward to a flow of commerce beyond these levels.
I trust that the resolution which is before us will find approval with all members of the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: REPORTED BAN ON FAREWELLS TO CREWS OF NORTHERN SUPPLY SHIPS
subtopic: RATIFICATION OF PROTOCOL RENEWING AGREEMENT WITH RUSSIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister has pointed out this resolution would give approval to a protocol between Canada and the Soviet union. Parliamentary approval, according to the convention although not of course the law of our constitution, is now required before any agreement between Canada and any other country can appropriately be ratified, that is any agreement of any substance or any agreement which imposes any obligations of any kind on the government and parliament of Canada. It would be interesting in this connection to know-perhaps the minister will be able to inform the house when he concludes the debate-whether the Soviet union has ratified this protocol. Ratification by the Soviet certainly does not involve the kind of .parliamentary consideration which we give here. The agreement was signed on April 25 of this year and it would be interesting, therefore, to know whether or not it has already been ratified by Russia.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it would be interesting to read the resolution in order to ascertain

exactly what we are being asked to approve. The resolution reads as follows:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the ratification by Canada of the protocol, signed at Moscow, on April IS, 1960, renewing the agreement on trade between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, concluded in Ottawa, on February 29, 1956, and that this house do approve the same.
There is in this resolution mention of the protocol alone. That is what we are being asked to approve and nothing else. If you read the protocol, Mr. Speaker-and the minister has referred to it-you will find that all it does is extend the agreement of 1956, with the exception of one article, namely article IX, which is the formal article at the end dealing with the coming into effect, the term of the agreement and that kind of thing. All we are being asked to do is extend the agreement of 1956, and to extend also the understanding set out in the letters which the two parties exchanged on the same date as the earlier agreement regarding the establishment of methods for valuing goods for duty.
We are asked to extend this former agreement and this particular exchange of letters between the two governments for another three years. No mention is made in this protocol of any other exchange of letters laying down the terms of trade between the two countries. Of course, Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house could not possibly object to the extension of the earlier agreement. It was an agreement that we negotiated. I think it is a satisfactory agreement so far as it goes in laying down the conditions of commercial relationships between the two countries. Naturally, then, we approve of its extension.
We also entirely approve of the extension of the exchange of letters which lay down the rules for valuation, an extremely important part-indeed an essential part-of any agreement dealing with trade with the Soviet union. But this new exchange of letters which lay down the terms of trade which are to prevail for three years after the date of the signature of the letters and which is not mentioned in the protocol is something else again. While we are not asked in this resolution to deal with or to approve or to disapprove of it, naturally, as the minister has made reference to it, it is not possible to talk about the protocol or approval of the protocol without discussing at the same time this other exchange which is not mentioned in the protocol but which does indeed deal with the terms of trade which are to exist between Canada and the Soviet union, if this agreement is ratified for the next three years.

When last April the minister announced in the house the signing of the agreement, he said that the arrangements set out in this exchange of letters were satisfactory to the government and he went on to add, and he repeated it today "taking into account changed trade conditions". The only change which the minister mentioned then, and I think I am right in saying this, was the change in the position of Russia as a wheat producer and exporter. Since 1956, when the earlier agreement was signed, there has been great development of agricultural production, particularly wheat production, in Russia. Acreage has greatly increased, and as a result Russia has become a potential exporter of wheat.
Of course Russia had been an exporter throughout this century. Even at the time when famine in Russia interfered with exports of wheat in the normal way, Russia was still exporting wheat. Indeed Russian imports and exports of wheat over the years have not always been determined by economic considerations. So the only change in trade conditions in that respect is perhaps, because of the new acreage brought under cultivation, that Russia may have more wheat to export in normal circumstances. But Russia, when it suits her economic or her political purposes, will import wheat, especially across the Pacific into the eastern provinces of Russia. It is more convenient and more economical at times for Russia to import wheat into those Pacific provinces than to move it from the European areas across Siberia.
The minister expressed the hope that this exchange of letters and of course the protocol would result in fruitful co-operation in trade between the two countries. He thought this exchange would make such fruitful co-operation possible. We have grave doubts whether this particular exchange of notes which is not, as I repeat, mentioned in the protocol will make possible the kind of fruitful cooperation which we would all like to see brought about.
The previous arrangement, as the minister has pointed out, came into effect on February 29, 1956 and lasted for three years. I had something to do with the negotiation of that arrangement. It was an interesting negotiation. It did not take very long. It was not too difficult. There was a meeting of a few days in Moscow, and Russian trade delegates came to Ottawa. There was some hard bargaining on both sides and the agreement was drawn up, signed and later approved in the House of Commons. There was quite an interesting debate in the house on that occasion.
The particular arrangement in the exchange of letters at that time was a far better one, as we see it, from the Canadian point of
Trade Agreement with Russia view than is the present arrangement in the exchange of letters which appear attached to the protocol. The minister has pointed out that under the earlier agreement, which was the basis of the trade relations, established, we gave Russia most favoured nation treatment. In doing so we put our commercial relationships with that country on a treaty basis. That, of course, is being continued in this new protocol.
There is, I think only one substantial change from the protocol from the earlier agreement. Section 2 of the protocol reads as follows:
Each of the two governments hereby affirms that it will give sympathetic consideration to any representations which the other government may make in respect to the implementation of this protocol and of other matters affecting their commercial relations.
In the earlier agreement those last words were not included, and the consultation that was provided for in the earlier agreement was limited to the implementation of the agreement itself. We on this side of the house certainly have no objection to that extension in paragraph 2. Perhaps a broadening of the basis of consultation at this time may be a good thing. Then the other paragraph of the protocol merely includes the section IX of the old agreement.
In the earlier exchange of letters which accompanied the 1956 agreement and to which the minister referred-I wish to refer to them, too, because I want to draw the contrast between the arrangement made then and the arrangement made in 1960, a contrast which I think is all to the disadvantage of Canada-the Soviet union agreed to buy, according to the exchange of letters on February 29, 1956, from Canada-
-during the three years dating from the signature of this agreement, between 1,200,000 and
1.500.000	metric tons of wheat in annual amounts of between 400,000 and 500,000 tons. The quantity of wheat between 400,000 and 500,000 tons purchased by the Soviet union during each of the second and third years of the validity of the agreement shall be finally determined with due account being taken of the volume of sales of Soviet goods in Canada and Canadian purchases thereof.
Mr. Speaker, it is on the record, and the minister has mentioned it, that over the term of the agreement the Soviet government failed to meet these objectives except in the first year of the agreement. I think when the agreement lapsed they were about
200.000	tons, some 8 million bushels, short. One would have thought that shortage on the part of the Soviet union would have given us something to bargain with when we were negotiating an extension of the arrangement and a new exchange of letters. This negotiation took a long time. I understand it took over a year; therefore there must have been some bargaining going on.

Trade Agreement with Russia But the result of that negotiation and that bargaining from our point of view on this side is very unsastisfactory in its effect on the possibility of extending Canadian trade, especially trade in wheat, with the Soviet union.
The figures for exports to Russia in the years of the agreement and subsequently are quite interesting. The year before the agreement was signed, in 1955, we exported to Russia $2,680,000 worth of commodities, all of which in that year was wheat. In 1956, after the agreement was signed, that figure went up from $2,680,000 to $24,605,000 and included almost $1 million of commodities other than wheat and 15 million bushels of wheat. In 1957 the figures went down, although still considerably above 1955, to $10,657,000, of which $9,057,000 was wheat. In 1958 wheat purchases from Canada by Russia amounted to $11,658,000 and there were other purchases of $7,209,000, which was mostly barley, making a total of nearly $19 million.
Last year, 1959, the wheat purchases were $10,787,000 and other purchases $1,953,000, making a total of $12,740,000 of Canadian exports to Russia. The commodities apart from wheat included in these figures were barley, which I have mentioned and which was very significant in 1958, some steel goods, some drugs and some chemicals. However, the fact remains that while after the first year the Russians did not meet their agreed purchases, the terms of trade during the three years of this agreement were four or five to one in our favour, and that is a fact which should be remembered when we consider the new exchange of letters.
The new protocol does not touch this situation, but the new exchange of letters certainly does. The minister has already read, and I will repeat, the really operative part of this letter of April 18, even though it is not, as I have said, part of the protocol or part of the documents referred to in the resolution of approval. Paragraph 3 of this letter signed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and addressed to the minister of foreign trade of the U.S.S.R. reads:
It is further understood that the ministry of foreign trade of the U.S.S.R., in accordance with its customary procedures, will see to it that Soviet foreign trade organizations each year during the three-year period from this date purchase in Canada, under normal commercial conditions, Canadian goods of their choice and which may be exported by Canada to a total value of 25 million Canadian dollars, including not less than 200,000 tons of Canadian wheat, provided-[DOT]
This proviso is the most important change between this exchange of letters and the other.
-the total annual value of Canadian purchases from the U.S.S.R. is not less than 12J million Canadian dollars. Should the total value of Canadian

purchases from the U.S.S.R. be less than 122 million Canadian dollars in any one year, the relationship between the value of such Canadian purchases and the value of those of the Soviet Union shall be in the ratio of 1 to 2; wheat will constitute not less than half of the value of the annual Soviet purchases.
It should be clear, Mr. Speaker, that in this exchange of letters there is no commitment on the part of the Soviet union to purchase any wheat in default under the earlier agreement, but there is a mathematical formula laying down the relationship, unless the maximum figures are realized as they have never been realized in the past, of exports to imports.
I do not know of any other case, although the minister will correct me if I am wrong, where we have accepted a trade arrangement with any foreign country on that basis, where we have limited ourselves in any way to any mathematical formula of exports versus imports. This was suggested to us in 1956 when we negotiated the earlier agreement with the Russians, and we would have no part of it.
How will this particular arrangement work out? Last year-and these were not abnormal figures-Canada bought from Russia only about $2J million worth of goods; furs, pig iron and some chrome were I think the main commodities. If this agreement is approved now, and if this exchange of letters becomes operative and if the figure for this year becomes more or less the same figure for last year, we would be able to export under this arrangement only $5 million worth of goods, of which half would be wheat. But even last year, the figures for which were well below the figures for 1957, as I have pointed out, we exported $12,750,000 worth of goods to Russia.
Therefore, in the light of past experience where are we going to get the Russian imports which would make possible under this arrangement our reaching even the figure we reached last year? To reach last year's figure alone we have to import $6 million worth of Russian goods. If we do not do that, under this exchange of letters we are practically inviting the Soviet union to reduce its purchases in Canada, especially purchases of wheat.
That is one very weak point indeed in this arrangement, this exchange of notes. I am not now talking about the protocol. Furthermore, the question arises as to how and when Russia will determine its purchases under the two for one provision. Is that going to be done at the end of each year and applied to the subsequent year? Is it going to be done in the middle of the year, or how is it going to be done? This kind of arrangement with a mathematical formula and without precise

details as to how it will be carried out will give rise to every opportunity for misunderstanding.
Surely it is particularly important when you are making an arrangement with a communist country, with a state-trading country, that everything should be perfectly clear in the documents you are signing. We have had lots of experience during the last 15 years in the political and economic fields; I am not thinking especially of Canada, but of other countries. We have much experience in the danger and disillusion and recrimination which arise as a result of signing documents with communist countries which mean one thing to them and another to us, and which because of their imprecise language can be interpreted in its own interest by the communist country during the course of the arrangements.
Notwithstanding this, however, the protocol says in its preamble that its purpose is to extend and diversify trade between the two countries. That is, of course, a purpose which we all support, but it is a purpose which we do not think will be realized in view of the exchange of letters about which I have been talking.
Are there any restrictions on our exports under this new arrangement? Well, yes. The security clause of the earlier arrangement has been retained, and it is most desirable that it should have been retained. Among other things it would prevent our exporting uranium to the Soviet union in case any minister of the crown should attempt to send Canadian uranium to that country. Are there any restrictions on our imports under this arrangement? We have not heard of any, except again, I suppose, in the security clause; there would have to be some limitation on imports if they were in any way prejudicial to the security of the country. It is not easy to see how that could arise in the case of imports, though they certainly might be prejudicial to the economic security of some of our manufacturing companies, and I am thinking particularly of the motor car manufacturing companies.
When the debate took place in this house on the earlier agreement in 1956, the present Minister of Finance was very much worried about the lack of restriction or limitation of any kind on imports, and in his contribution to the debate in 1956, as reported on page 3045 of Hansard, the hon. gentleman had this to say:
I think it is to be deplored that there is no guarantee in this agreement that Canada shall not be asked to import goods manufactured by forced labour behind the iron curtain. By this agreement-
Trade Agreement with Russia
That is the earlier agreement.
-it is entirely left to Canadian purchasers to assure themselves if they choose to do so that the goods they are purchasing from Russia are not goods manufactured by forced labour.
The Minister of Finance was very preoccupied with that question at that time. Well, he had an opportunity in the course of the negotiations preceding this agreement to put something along those lines into the new protocol, if he desired to do so, but there is no indication that any steps were taken to that end.
The present Minister of Finance was also very worried at that time about the danger of espionage as a result of signing an agreement at that time and he said, further, on page 3046:
The fourth matter to which I draw attention, in trying to bring about a sound and fair understanding of the agreement and what it contains, as well as its limitations, is the danger that wherever Russian trade organizations go there is always the danger of espionage.
I do not know whether that danger worried the minister when he was considering this particular agreement. My hon. friend from Essex East recalls also the statement made by the Minister of Finance at that time concerning the treatment of the merchant marine, which is covered in one of the paragraphs of the present protocol extending the same provision in the earlier agreement. None of the matters which caused so much anxiety to the Minister of Finance at that time-an anxiety which he expressed in strong terms in this House of Commons-seems to have worried him in connection with the extension of the agreement in the form we have before us.
To sum up, naturally we support the protocol and the exchange of notes dealing with valuation, which are the only two things we are asked to support in this resolution; but, as it has been brought into the discussion, we must say that we do not think that the exchange of notes which lays down the terms of trade between the two countries is a satisfactory one from the Canadian point of view.
This is a bad bargain. We would be in favour of any agreement which would extend Canadian trade, because nothing is much more important to our economic prosperity, our stability and even our existence than an expanding external trade. We would be particularly anxious to support an agreement which would open up new markets for our wheat exports, but we object to this particular exchange of notes, this two to one formula, both because of the principle of accepting a formula of this kind, which we think is undesirable, and also because we think the result of this exchange of notes is

Trade Agreement with Russia likely to be not an expansion but a limitation of our exports, particularly of our wheat exports.
Therefore, though the protocol is satisfactory and the exchange of notes mentioned in the resolution is satisfactory, this particular exchange lays down an undesirable principle of two to one by which we shall be bound during the currency of this agreement. That particular exchange cannot be approved on this side of the house because, instead of expanding, it is more likely to limit trade.

speechtext:
The resolution before the house to approve the terms of the new trade agreement betweeen Canada and the U.S.S.R. deserves, of course, serious consideration. Canada's trade generally in recent years has been posing many problems for our most important industries. Many of the export industries of this country are finding it more difficult to obtain markets, and more difficult to hold the markets they have had in the past. It is exceedingly necessary that the Canadian government should do everything possible to improve and expand Canada's trade.
It is true that written into this agreement is a two to one formula which binds the U.S.S.R. to buy from us a maximum of $25 million worth of goods in a year but only if we purchase from the Soviet union goods equal in value to 50 per cent of that amount. The Leader of the Opposition has spoken for the Liberal party, and he has said that this is a bad bargain. It may not, on the face of it, be a bargain as good as the 1956 agreement appeared to be on its face, but I think it is very unrealistic to think we can go on exporting to any country in the world on the basis of four times as much as we buy, or to export six or seven times as much as we are prepared to buy from that country. On the basis of the ratio of trade and, I think, on the basis of absolute trade, it seems to me that our position vis-a-vis the United States is a much worse bargain than the formula contained in the agreement now under consideration. Our imports from the United States for the year ending December, 1959 amounted to $3.8 billion, but our exports in that year fell short of this amount by some $700 million, being just in excess of $3.1 billion.
No one can compare the value and size of Canada's trade with the United States with the trade we have had with the U.S.S.R., but I think it is a little far fetched to say that a two to one ratio in Canada's favour is, on the face of it, a bad bargain. I do not think we should attempt to say that an agreement with the U.S.S.R. or any communist nation is on


the face of it a bad bargain, but I wonder if that is not the stand taken by the Leader of the Opposition.

see a better formula and more exports covered by the agreement, we think the agreement itself is a valuable one and should be supported. We think it is in the interests of Canada. I am not talking about absolute equality, but I think it is a perfectly ridiculous position to take, as the Leader of the Opposition has done, that the ratio of from four to one up to eleven to one in Canada's favour is something that can be maintained as a practical proposition in trading with a great country like the U.S.S.R. If we were able to have a two to one formula and bring about a two to one result in our trade with other important countries, then the talk about an adverse trade balance would be forgotten and this problem would be solved.
The reduction in the amount of wheat that will be sold under this agreement is serious, but in spite of the fact that the agreement does not hold out the possibility of the same kind of large exports of this commodity as under the former agreement we say that if this is the best bargain the Canadian government could obtain, we are pleased that the government has agreed to the agreement subject to parliamentary approval, and we are pleased to lend our support to that approval.

speechtext:
I am rather surprised that the Leader of the Opposition should take the stand he has taken because, as the hon. member for Assiniboia has pointed out, what happened was that the U.S.S.R. entered into a trade agreement with the former administration under which they got badly burned to the tune of four or five to one and in certain years ten to twelve to one. In the light of that experience, when they came to sign the new agreement they said they must have a better deal, and I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce has done a good job in getting this two for one agreement. I cannot see that a two for one agreement is not good.

I should like to put on the record a few trading figures which indicate a much worse situation than that mentioned by the hon. member for Assiniboia. What do hon. members think of a trading arrangement whereby in 1959 Canada imported crude oil from Arabia to the value of $70 million whereas our total exports were under $3 million? This is a ratio of $1 of imports to 4 cents of sales. In 1959 we had imports from the Netherlands Antilles amounting to $47 million, almost all of which comprised petroleum products, while total exports were slightly over $1 million, or a ratio of $1 of imports to a little over 2 cents in sales. If you take Venezuela you will find that the ratio was $1 of imports to 22 cents of sales. These make the discrepancies talked about in the trade agreement with the U.S.S.R. look like chicken feed.
With regard to whether, as the Leader of the Opposition said, we are going to make a success of this trade agreement, what are we going to import? I read in one of the Toronto newspapers that an importer of motor cars had cancelled an order for some 500 automobiles. I can imagine what our automobile manufacturers and their employees would say if we started importing motor cars from a state-trading nation. We hear a lot of talk today about importing motor cars from low wage countries. What are the costs of manufacture in a state-trading nation? What would happen to the shoe manufacturers if we imported shoes? What would happen to the oil industry if we imported gasoline? We had an instance of that.
It appears that about the only thing we can import from the Russians is raw or semi-processed material of which we happen to be short in this country or which could be landed in geographical areas of the country to which our own production could not be transported economically. One item which was mentioned was chrome, and another item starting with "c" which might be mentioned would be caviar. I think we could soon exhaust the list of things which might be imported under this trading agreement. However, there is one commodity, and that is oil. This oil might be imported into areas which are not now served by western crude but which are served solely by imported crude. I have given illustrations of our imbalance of trade with various countries. If we only transferred 10 per cent of our oil imports from Saudi Arabia to the Russians we would not be displacing one barrel of western crude, and this move would immediately ensure the success of this agreement.
However, we cannot do this because no matter at what price oil is offered, there is 79951-0-386J
Trade Agreement with Russia no such thing as a free market in so far as oil is concerned. There is such a thing as commercial preference. When the oil companies are importing from foreign countries they only import oil which they own themselves. These companies will not import other oil unless they are told to do so by the government, as they are in every other country except Canada. I say it is time we took a look at the oil industry. It is time that we, as a government, imposed quotas. The imposition of quotas would help our western production. This would also make it possible to assign quotas to the U.S.S.R. or any other nation with which we wanted to promote trade.
As the hon. member for Assiniboia said, the export of wheat is a major part of the activity of the harbour of Vancouver. We have noticed during the last year a lessening of activity as a result of the dropping off of our transpacific trade. There will be exports of pulp because the Russians are not yet selfsustaining in pulp, as well as other products which come from our exporting industries of the west. It is very difficult for a nation such as Canada, dedicated to the proposition that trade shall be in private hands and that only in very restricted areas shall the government intervene, to trade with a state-trading nation. As I pointed out earlier, any trade in consumer goods will rouse a storm of protest from whatever industrial areas might be affected.
However, we do have this area in which we could move and in which we could make this trading agreement a 100 per cent success. Incidentally, we could show the major world oil companies that the government of this country is greater than they are. The method by which these companies operate is international in scope and has no regard for the over-all welfare or economic well-being of this country. The other day in the house, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Calgary South, the minister said he was going to take a look at the oil industry now that we have the final report of the Borden commission. This government deserves credit for having set up the Borden commission and the energy board. There was no movement in this area under the previous regime. The movement in this area which would ensure the success of this trade treaty, which would have value to the U.S.S.R. as well as to ourselves, was not taken by the previous administration. They hooked the Russians and the Russians have reacted in a typical manner, even though their reactions are still in our favour.
I say therefore, Mr. Speaker, that if any of the oil companies would like to show some public spirit, without government intervention, they could, by reducing their imports

Trade Agreement with Russia of oil from Saudi Arabia by 10 per cent and diverting this to the U.S.S.R., ensure the success of this treaty.

The Leader of the Opposition now claims I have not read the protocol. May I assure him that I have done my homework. I have to agree with him that there are matters in the protocol that I should like to amend. However, I believe that on the whole it is a good thing that we have reached an agreement with the U.S.S.R.
I am willing to support the renewal of the agreement. He does not like the agreement, but he is going to vote for it. I do not know where, except on the political platform, he is going to express his utter disagreement with what has been done. I believe the electors will realize, at that time, just what his argument is. It is merely for political reasons
fMr. Broome.]

that the official opposition is expressing its opposition. However, when it comes down to brass tacks they are going to vote in favour of the motion.
I have never been overly optimistic about the possibilities of Canadian prosperity being enhanced by trading relationships with nations whose natural resources and enterprises are so much like ours. I have always maintained that the welfare of the Canadian economy is not primarily dependent upon our trading relationships with either the United States of America or the U.S.S.R. Those nations have a great deal of pulp and paper, plenty of wheat and plenty of all those things that we should like to export.
I feel it is wrong for the Canadian economy to be so dependent upon nations whose natural resources are so much like our own. I believe that our future economic welfare would be more enhanced if we had more active trading relationships with nations such as the West Indies federation, India, China, the United Kingdom or the countries of western Europe, in other words countries which are not our natural competitors with regard to the products we may have in excess supply and available for export.
I do not place any undue optimism on the results of the agreement now before us. However, to say that this is a bad bargain raises another issue. I realize that it may well be a bad bargain in comparison with the old agreement. However, I believe all of us are adult enough and have at our disposal information enough that we ought to realize that we could not expect the old agreement to be continued indefinitely with any beneficial results to the Canadian economy. After all, whenever any other government offers to buy $2 worth of goods from us if we will buy $1 worth from them, according to my way of looking at things that is a good bargain; it is basically a good bargain, even though it may not be as excellent a bargain as that which we may have had previously.
My real reason for participating in this debate is that I know of a number of Canadian enterprises that are very much involved in and very much concerned with the success of this agreement, notably the wheat producers. To be willing to brush aside the sale of millions of bushels of Canadian wheat merely because we are no longer getting the bargain we used to enjoy is, I feel, rather irresponsible action. However, when the government undertook to agree to this new deal with the U.S.S.R., I hope it also realized its own responsibility.
The agreement makes it plain that the U.S.S.R. is obligated to buy only $2 worth of goods for every $1 worth of goods that we

buy. I should like to hear that the government realizes its responsibilities in this regard. I feel it is rather vain to hope that Canadian private enterprise is going to make any unusual move toward an increase in our imports from the U.S.S.R. The only way in which we can increase or even hold the level of our exports is if we are to import a considerable volume of goods from the U.S.S.R.
I should like to recommend to the minister that he not resort to wishful thinking in this regard, and that he not rely overly much on making a number of pious appeals in meetings that he may hold with Canadian importers. I should like to advocate that he use remedies that are at hand, that he use the export and import permits legislation and also the facilities of the Canadian Commercial Corporation. If he uses the Export and Import Permits Act and the Canadian Commercial Corporation, I feel he will be able to realize a level of imports that will help Canadian exporters to maintain or even to enhance the level of exports that we have had hitherto.
In other words, I am asking him not to rely for results once again, as has so often occurred in the past, on platitudes and pious appeals in addressing chambers of commerce and the like across the nation. I am asking that the government realize that it has undertaken an obligation. I am saying that if it intends to implement not only the letter but the spirit of this agreement the government has a direct responsibility in this regard, and that the government, if necessary, ought to resort to the legislative authority it now has in order that we may be assured of an adequate level of imports from the U.S.S.R. to the end that Canadian exporters and especially Canadian wheat producers may not be obliged to suffer the penalties of the new agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate, but I was following it very closely this morning and I could not understand why there seemed to be the desire on the part of the two members of the C.C.F. who spoke to misinterpret what I thought had been so clearly stated by the Leader of the Opposition in his analysis of the protocol which is before us, and the position of this party thereon. The Leader of
Trade Agreement with Russia the Opposition pointed out that in substance the new protocol is simply bringing back into force a protocol of a trade agreement that was negotiated by the previous administration, and consequently it would be difficult to quarrel with that.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make very clear what it is that we are being asked to vote upon. The resolution is very short and simple, as is the protocol, and I think both should be on the record in view of what was said just before the adjournment. The resolution simply states:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the ratification by Canada of the protocol, signed at Moscow, on April 18, 1960, renewing the agreement on trade between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, concluded in Ottawa, on February 29, 1956, and that this house do approve the same.
There is nothing there whatever about letters, or a two for one formula, or anything of that nature. The hon. member for Assini-boia and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam were both challenged by the Leader of the Opposition and asked to read the formula. They would not do so, but I will do so because again it is a very short and very clear document. It reads as follows:
In connection with the expiration of the Canadian-Soviet trade agreement concluded in Ottawa on February 29, 1956, for a period of three years, the government of Canada and the government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, desiring to expand and diversify further the trade between the two countries on the basis of mutual advantage, have agreed as follows:
Then this is the pertinent section which is before us:
With the exception of article IX, the trade agreement between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics of February 29, 1956, as well as the understanding set out in the letters which the two parties exchanged on the same date regarding the establishment of values of goods for duty, are hereby extended for a period of three years from the date of signature of this protocol.
Mr. Speaker, let me refer to these words "as well as the understanding". The understanding with respect to values for duty was something which had relation to the exchange of letters in 1956. If it were part of the protocol it would certainly not be necessary specifically to bring back in this language a reference to agreement on a continuance of this understanding.
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the minister is not considering amending the resolution before us if he wants to make clear what this house is approving, because it simply says that we are being asked to approve this protocol. This protocol has nothing to do with letters, and the one in 1956 has nothing to do with letters, or we would not be specifically asked to bring back not.

Trade Agreement with Russia all the letters which refer to the 1956 agreement but only letters on one subject. The resolution differs from the resolution in 1956 because then, instead of being asked to approve a protocol, we were asked to approve an agreement on trade.
That, I think, for the record sets out the position of this party. We have no quarrel with the bringing back of the agreement in so far as it is part of a protocol such as was negotiated in 1956. This party does feel that the two for one formula is unique and undesirable. However, in our opinion that is not what we are being asked to approve in the language of the resolution before us.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I note with interest that there is general approval of the resolution now before the house, with some minor criticisms on the part of members of the opposition, and full approval by the C.C.F. representatives.
The Leader of the Opposition started off by asking whether the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics had ratified the agreement. This question did not bother him four years ago when he was discussing the trade agreement with the U.S.S.R., on April 18, 1956. As reported on page 3055 of Hansard for that date he said:
For instance, we are today asking in the House of Commons to approve ratification of this treaty. In Soviet practice no such approval is, of course, required and, indeed, legally and constitutionally under our own system no such approval is required because ratification is an executive act.
Then he went on to explain the difference between our two systems of government.
The hon. member for Eglinton, who was spokesman for the opposition of that day, was also aware of the practice and as reported on page 3042 of Hansard for April 18, 1956 he said:
We are told that under the Russian practice the signing of the agreement by their authorized officers itself constitutes ratification on the part of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
So perhaps we are clear on that point. There will be, as stated in the protocol itself, an exchange of instruments of ratification. The third article of the protocol reads in this way:
This protocol shall be ratified by both contracting parties as soon as possible and shall enter into force provisionally on the date of its signature and definitively on the date of exchange of the instruments of ratification which shall take place in Ottawa.
There was some discussion about the nature of the resolution which is before us. The

word "protocol" was used because this is a renewal of an agreement on trade between Canada and the U.S.S.R. I do not see that we could have written that this was an agreement renewing an agreement without some question arising as to the use of language. Let us look at the resolution which was before the House of Commons in 1956. It read:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament approve the ratification by Canada of the agreement on trade between Canada and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, signed at Ottawa, on February 29, 1956, and that this house do approve the same.
There was no mention there of any letters which were exchanged at that time. On this occasion there were two such letters, one from Mr. N. S. Patolichev to me and one from me to him. On that other occasion four letters were exchanged, but they were not mentioned in the resolution subsequently placed before the house. When the spokesman for the opposition of that day, the hon. member for Eglinton, was speaking he said:
In approaching the resolution now under debate I take it that we are entitled to look at all five documents, for certainly the letters have extremely high importance for us in our approach to the question of ratification and approval of the treaty.
So today we may look at all three documents, or if you like at all four-the letters I have mentioned, the protocol and the agreement of 1956-and it is reasonable to expect that the house, in looking at all the documents, will be expressing its approval of all the documents when the debate is concluded.
In criticizing the change which has been made in the amount of wheat which is to be purchased by Russia the Leader of the Opposition said in effect that the only change which had taken place in the four years was a change in Russia's own wheat position, that Russia had now become an exporter of wheat. I mentioned some other changes. I said in the course of my remarks this morning that since 1956 the Soviet union has concluded a number of trade agreements with non-communist countries under which they have avoided giving unilateral and unconditional purchase commitments. The Soviet Republic, as I understand it, has enlarged its trading obligations throughout the world and has signed a great many agreements with various countries; and it is interesting to note, as I think was pointed out by the hon. member for Assiniboia, that Canada is the only country with which Russia has made an agreement of this nature on a two to one basis.
This two to one basis was subjected to criticism by the Leader of the Opposition, but none of the other Soviet trade agreements of which I am aware are on that basis at all;

they are on a one for one basis, and when I was talking to the Russian ministers they informed me that their objective was to balance their trade with other countries. We talked about the advantages of multi lateral trading and balancing a surplus with one country against a deficit with another. On a world-wide basis that proves to be satisfactory in many instances. However, they said that their plan, at least for the time being, was to attempt to get a balance country by country. When that is their method of doing business with other countries, to offer a two to one ratio is a concession which goes considerably beyond what Russia is doing elsewhere.
The Leader of the Opposition called it a bargain. It was a bad bargain, he said, because the amount of wheat to be purchased by Russia is not as great as it was under the former agreement. It is true that it is not as great. It is half the size of the annual purchase agreed upon under the former arrangement, but conditions have changed since then. Russia has had greater success in the production of wheat in the last four years and is now, as has been mentioned, an exporter of wheat; she does not rely upon Canadian wheat from the standpoint of her existence. As was pointed out in 1956, and as has been pointed out again by the hon. member for Assiniboia, it is just cheaper economically to get wheat from Vancouver and ship it to Vladivostok than it is to rail wheat from the Ukraine and transport it by way of the Trans-Siberian railway.
The Russian minister said exactly that to me. They do not really require our wheat. It is not that they are suffering from a shortage of food. It is just a matter of convenience; it is a little easier on some occasions to get wheat by water than by rail, just as two years ago Australia purchased wheat from Canada at a time when they had a partial crop failure. It was easier to take it by sea from Vancouver to the northern part of Australia than it was to transport it from southern Australia to the areas that needed it.
Although there has been a reduction in the amount of wheat to be sold to Russia under this agreement, the amount involved is nevertheless an important quantity. As has been mentioned, with the competitive position of Canada in the world wheat trade being challenged, seven and a half million bushels is important in our total exports of wheat. I suggest to the hon. member for Assiniboia that when he calls Canada the second exporter of wheat in the world he should revise that phrase and state, as is the fact, that Canada is the first, the leading,
Trade Agreement with Russia world exporter of wheat in commercial markets. The export of wheat by the United States is to a very large extent not on a commercial basis. Non-commercial exports amount this year to over 70 per cent. In many instances the wheat is given away as an outright gift or under long term arrangements, or it is sold for local currency. Canada is still the world's leading exporter of wheat in commercial markets. Russia may be creeping up as a competitor in that field, because the Russian need for wheat is not as great as it may have appeared several years ago, hence the reduction in the amount of wheat which that country has suggested she would take under this new agreement.
There is a misunderstanding, I think, with regard to the two to one formula. That is the minimum figure. It is not a restriction. Once trade between the two countries is in ratio- $12.5 million on the one side and $25 million on the other side-it will be on a one to one basis. It does not continue on a two to one basis indefinitely in total figures. It does not cause a restriction in trade simply because Russia suggests that she will measure her imports from Canada on the basis of her exports to Canada.

Some question was raised as to whether it would have been wiser to have required Russia to complete her purchases of wheat for the year 1959, when her purchases fell short by about 7 million bushels, prior to signing the trade agreement. I did consider that, and thought it might not be wise to insist at that particular time on the fulfillment of that former agreement; but I took the opportunity to press the point that it would be advisable to complete that agreement of 1959 so we could move on into this new agreement with each party having confidence in the other.
I observe that in 1956 the Leader of the Opposition, who was then secretary of state

Trade Agreement with Russia for external affairs, looked forward to that point concerning whether or not the obligations would be fulfilled by each country. These are his words, as reported at page 3056 of Hansard of April 18, 1956:
It may be asked-whether the Soviet union will carry out the obligation which it has undertaken to Canada with respect to wheat purchases. I think we may have confidence that it will do so. Selfinterest, if no other reason, would dictate that it should do so. Apart from its need for wheat, a failure to do so would damage its international reputation in trade matters-
I used somewhat similar words in talking this over with the Russian representatives. I thought it would be good business on their part to pick up very quickly that balance of 7 million bushels which we had hoped they would take last year. Had they taken it last year we would have reached the 300 million bushels of exports which were our target. I feel reasonably certain that when we complete the ratification of this protocol the Russians will make up that deficiency. I could not have received more firm assurances in that respect without actually having a document written and signed. I did not think it was necessary to go to that extreme, of putting everything down in writing.
The Leader of the Opposition has spoken of the necessity of having documents very carefully written and examined for phraseology because of misunderstanding, particularly in dealing with some countries. In this instance we feel that the agreement of 1956 together with the protocol and letters accompanying it were explicit. I have left it to the good will of the Russian representatives with whom I talked to make up that slight drop in the agreement for the purchase of wheat over the preceding three years. I am inclined to place reliance on the word they gave me. I would also be inclined to judge the value of the present extension of the agreement by whether or not that former agreement is fulfilled to its limit.
Seven million bushels of wheat is not a very large amount in terms of Russian trade nor in terms of Canadian trade. It is interesting to note that Canadian total trade, exports and imports, running over $10 billion a year are just about the same as Russian total trade, exports and imports, running over $10 billion a year. As I recall it the Russians look with some surprise and perhaps a little envy at a country of 18 million people having an export and import trade equal in dollar value and volume to that of Russia, a country of 200 million people.
Whether the agreement is as good as the one of 1956 remains to be seen. I think we have moved a little way along the road toward expanding trade with Russia. Here is an incentive. Dollar purchases on the part


of Canadian businessmen will be met on the part of Russian businessmen with two dollar purchases from Canada. It is up to the businessmen of both countries to see what they can do to expand trade.
Mr. Patolichev told me in our conversation, "We know you have things to sell other than wheat, but that is all we hear about". We did not name specific articles. He spoke about the development of their country and what other foreign importers were doing with regard to establishing manufacturing plants in Russia and things of that nature. He said, "I am familiar with most of the leading businessmen of Sweden, for example, which of course is quite close. I do not, however, know any Canadian businessmen, certainly not on the same terms". We agreed that there had not been that intermingling of businessmen between our two countries that is essential if trade is to expand. This then led to the suggestion that there should be an exchange of trade missions of businessmen between both countries, and that may well happen during the course of this year. It is through the activity of businessmen on both sides that business will develop.
The state trading organization in Russia has to be understood by Canadian businessmen. We have stationed in Moscow now a trade commissioner who is making himself familiar with Russian trading practices and will pass on that information to Canadian businessmen. I was informed that once a year the Russians set up their quotas and objectives with regard to trade with each country for the year, and then the books are more or less closed so you have to strike while the iron is hot if trade is to be accomplished. I do not know to what extent that situation prevails, or whether there is a modification during the course of the year; nevertheless the methods used by a statetrading nation differ from those of a private enterprise country.
I cannot go along with the representatives of the C.C.F. in suggesting, as I understood them to suggest, that the government might do more and that the government's responsibility was greater than it is concerning trade with Russia or any other state-trading country. The government cannot do more than lay the framework and the basis for trade, get the treaties negotiated and signed, open offices where commercial counsellors are available, and assist businessmen as they travel back and forth by passing on information to the businessmen. That is a function of government, but it is up to the businessmen themselves to form their own judgment as to what articles they are going to export or what articles they are going to import. It is not a

responsibility of the government to do that. It is a government responsibility to protect the trading community from the dumping of goods and things of that nature, but other than that not much more can be done in a private enterprise country with regard to trading relations with a state-trading country. It is up to the businessmen of both countries to become active and to enlarge our trade.
Similar words to these were spoken in 1956 by Mr. Howe, who was then minister of trade and commerce. He did not hold out too much hope with regard to trade with Russia, but he certainly put the emphasis and responsibility on the businessmen if that trade was going to expand. I cannot find the reference at this moment.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few brief remarks on this bill.
As the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) said, the first section of the bill is necessary mostly on account of the fact that the government has allowed the sale to the general public of 22-inch guns commonly called "Hornet Survival Rifles".

Here is something which appeared in the November 22, 1958 issue of the Montreal Star, and I quote:
Halt Distribution
Crown Assets at any rate stopped distribution of the rifles. The declarations of surplus were sent back to the defence department last February 13.
Then the air force decided it thought the rifles dangerous but couldn't classify them as defective.
Crown Assets, on the other hand, wouldn't ban them from public sale unless they were classified to be scrapped.
A little further down, the article went on to say:
When on March 31 they got the declarations back classifying the rifles as either "new" or "used" but all "serviceable", the corporation went ahead with distribution.

And further down still:
-and that the rifles be sold only "for sporting purposes".
(Translation):
If there was a possibility that those rifles or shotguns could be dangerous, apart from being inefficient, I wonder why the department concerned allowed their being sold to the public, thus making necessary this bill which otherwise could have been dispensed with.
There has certainly been a mistake, either in the Department of National Defence, or in the Department of Defence Production.
If those guns were not dangerous, but just useless for regular service, I think the Department of Defence might have kept them as equipment for the Royal Canadian Air Force, army or navy cadets, for drilling purposes.
If some foresight had been shown, those shotguns would not have been put in the hands of people who like to play with firearms and endanger peoples' lives.
May I recall that my fellow member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) asked some questions in this regard, on January 20 and 22 as well as on February 3. An answer was put on the order paper, indicating all the figures I quoted a few moments ago.

the law, and it will become illegal to own such items.

We believe also that for one government agency to sell a person such a weapon in good faith, then later on discover it should not have been sold and retroactively determine that possession of such a weapon is a crime, is something which under normal circumstances should not be countenanced. However, in this case, as was said earlier, we do have a responsibility to society to assure that all possible steps are taken to protect society against persons who may use such weapons in bank robberies or other crimes against society.
For these reasons we do feel it is necessary to enact this legislation. We hope that in future the Department of National Defence,

Crown Assets Disposal Corporation or whatever body is in the process of disposing of surplus or unusable army equipment such as this will be a bit more careful in determining whether such articles should or should not be sold.
In so far as the use of sound recording equipment, tape recorders, is concerned in judicial proceedings under the Criminal Code, may I say that as science advances we become more amenable to accepting tape recorders in areas in which they have not normally been accepted. There is one thing that should be said in connection with the use of tape recorders, though I am not suggesting that this will occur if such recorders are used in proceedings before a justice. I am not suggesting this would be done or could be done with the use of such equipment in court, but if we are thinking in terms of extending the use of tape recorders and accepting what is on tape recorders when it is taken outside of court and possibly used in evidence, I think we should draw the line very definitely and should not allow such things as the splicing that can be done and the editing and the distortion of comments of the individual in order to suit any particular purpose.
