speechtext:
The point I want to bring up is perhaps a theoretical one, but it is always what I understood happened in appeal proceedings when the court was considering a transcript of the evidence. I have always had grave doubt about the fairness of such a transcript as compared with a recording. I think it is obvious in this House of Commons that a speech as given and the same speech as read are two different things, and it is possible to form a judgment of evidence of witnesses from a recording which one cannot get from a printed record.
I know this is perhaps a new interpretation to put on the matter, but I wonder if this might not be a step along the way finally to giving consideration, especially in appeal hearings, to a recording of the proceedings, because to me it gives a much more complete picture of what took place in the court room than does just the bare, flat record. I realize that this might introduce something completely new into the consideration of appeals, but I wondered whether anything like that was in the mind of the minister. It seems to me that it might begin to open the way toward that end, which I think might have some merit.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REPORTED BAN ON FAREWELLS TO CREWS OF NORTHERN SUPPLY SHIPS
subsubtopic: USE OF RECORDING MACHINES
speechtext:
I hardly think this could be described as a step in that direction, because that certainly is not the intent with which it is introduced. It is introduced as a matter in part of convenience and as a matter in part of making for greater accuracy in the recording of evidence or the addresses delivered in court. It is after all the function of the trial court to form an impression and make a finding based on their belief as to the veracity of a witness. They have the witnesses before them and that is one of the functions of the trial judge and/or the jury, the trial court in general.
Then again, in general but not exclusively, appeals to courts of appeal are usually taken on questions of law, although there may be questions of mixed fact and law. But it is not the function of the court of appeal as a general matter to come to an opinion as to the veracity of witnesses, because they always take the view, and rightly, that the trial court is in a much better position to come to that conclusion having had the witnesses before them. So in that sense the hearing of a sound impression of the whole proceeding is not as important to the court of appeal as it is to the trial court.
What is important to the court of appeal is an accurate record of what was said by witnesses and counsel, and indeed by the
Canada Elections Act
judge himself in giving his summing up, because they have to look at that from the point of view, generally speaking, of whether there are any errors in procedure or in points of law which would warrant their reversing the verdict below or the ordering of a new trial.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad the minister has given us the assurance that the bill corresponds to the committee's report, because I think it ought to limit the debate a good deal in the committee, that in fact the bill the government is going to introduce does not deviate in any respect whatsoever from the report of the committee, which was unanimous, as some reports have not been in this parliament.
The fact that it was unanimous, of course, does not mean that the committee was unanimous about some of the things that some of us thought ought to be in the elections act and are not. While I am arguing that it is expedient as a half loaf to accept what the minister is now recommending to us, speaking for myself, and in one or two respects also I think for my party-but in some respects I do not feel I am authorized to speak for anyone but myself, and I will try to indicate when I do and when I do not-I do not think we can regard this as any more than a relatively good job of tinkering.
There is one respect in which we in the Liberal party feel that we have a definite grievance. We did put forward a suggestion which was previously put forward by hon. members now supporting the government, as well as some hon. members who were in opposition in other days but who are no longer here. I admit at once that the amendment that was suggested in previous committees by the Conservatives was not accepted by the majority of that day; but as I have said, there are some Liberals who have the capacity to learn and we think we have learned something in this and other respects.
We think that the suggestion which was put forward by some very distinguished Conservatives in the past was a sound one. We were astonished, to put it mildly, that they should decide that they did not want to go on with what they had advocated over the years. What I refer to is the proposal that just as urban enumerators are nominated, one by the successful candidate and the other by the person who was the runner up in the election, so at rural polls should deputy returning officers be nominated by the successful candidate and the poll clerks by the unsuccessful candidate.
The reason this suggestion was put forward is that there are a good many parts of Canada in the rural areas, and especially the outlying areas such as exist in some of the constituencies in Newfoundland, in the constituency

of the hon. member for Kenora-iRainy River, no doubt in the constituency of the hon. member for Port Arthur, of the hon. member for Gatineau and a good many others, where it is difficult to get local people to be scrutineers for reasons into which I do not think it is necessary to enter at this time.
We felt that in order to remove any suggestion that the election machinery was controlled by any one party or group, this would be an improvement right in line with the spirit of the act as it now stands; and right in line, too, with the policy which has been followed for many years by the Conservative party. If it were possible to persuade the Acting Secretary of State even at this late date to see the light which was seen in the past by the members of his party and include this change, we think it would be a good thing; because it would be another assurance, of which we can never have too many, that our election machinery is in every respect above reproach.
I think most of us in the committee agreed that the federal election machinery, whatever some of us may think about some other jurisdictions, and that is not the business of this house, is on the whole not only very efficient but also, when properly carried out, very fair indeed. This is one way in which an additional assurance can be given.
There is another reason for doing this which should commend itself to every hon. member of this house who is concerned, as I know many of us are, with the steady increase in legitimate election expenses. It does seem to me that if we are going to preserve truly representative government, something much more serious and much more fundamental than has been done up to now will have to be done about the steadily mounting cost of elections, a large part of which is, of course, competitive; one party is forced to do it because another party does it.

Speaking for myself, I hope the day will come, and come soon, when broadcasting both by radio and television during election campaigns will be an entirely public matter and it will no longer be possible for anyone to purchase time for such broadcasts. So long as the purchase of time is permitted, the advantage, providing the person is a good broadcaster, is simply given to whoever has the longest purse. Without strings attached. Every hon. member is aware of how much it costs to fight an election. One hon. member recently told me he still owes money from the 1957 election. I know the situation in Port Arthur. One will never vouch for the expenses of anyone else, but I do know that our group has had to raise its sights for federal elections as between 1945 and 1960 from approximately $2,000 to approximately $6,000. Since our organization has never paid scrutineers or people to work in committee rooms I suppose you could estimate that the actual cost if these people were paid would be somewhere in the neighbourhood of $10,000 for our candidate. This seems to be a fairly average figure that would apply in most constituencies, at least in English speaking Canada.
I agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that much of the expense of election candidates is created by competition. As the election approaches the poor citizen reaches the saturation point. He gets fed up with spot announcements on the radio, big blurbs in the newspapers, sound trucks blaring and posters strung all over the place. Much of the competition between candidates tends to cancel itself out, and the citizens become fed up as election day nears. It is for this reason that I think the British have set a good example for us.
I am always glad to remind the Prime Minister of something about which he is fond of telling us, his love and respect for British institutions and the way the British do things. In Great Britain they have set definite limits on campaign expenses, and on the whole it seems to have worked out very well. The two major parties there, although I do not think one could say they trust each other, tend to have a respect for the various expenses declared. I cannot see why we could not do something like that in Canada.
The suggestion has been made that we might find it easier to meet this problem of restraint on the national level than on the local level so far as the national parties are concerned. It seems to me it will be some years before you can restrain in any constituency the natural enthusiasm of the candidate. One way it could be restrained would be to put something in the Canada Elections Act that would introduce a rather severe punishment for candidates who do not pay their election bills. This has always been a sore point in our part of the country. I do not know if it is a sore point in the rest of Canada. After the election the newspapers, radio stations, printers and people like that are always dunning candidates and complaining about their failure to pay up.
Many think it unfair that during an election campaign a candidate has to pay the national rate for advertising in any newspaper in Canada even though the candidate is advertising within the local framework. I have been told that the reason for this is the failure of candidates to pay their bills promptly. This has always seemed particularly vicious to me, but it has been caused by the fact that some of us have not been good at paying our bills promptly. Perhaps we might get some adjustment there and emerge from an election financially ahead. The situation where we are paying up to two or two and a half times for local advertising seems to me to be most unfair especially when the setting up of political advertising, as done by a candidate at the constituency level, is not a difficult proposition for the newspapers. The same situation

tends to apply so far as radio is concerned. Television is a somewhat different matter. I assume that the proposition put forward by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate with respect to the division of radio time not being done by the board of broadcast governors but under a provision in the act is a party proposition.

I refer to the whole question of redistribution. I know this is not a matter that comes under this act but it certainly seems to me it would be a question that would have relation to this particular committee. I think we are all very interested in knowing whether there is any intention of introducing a basic floor such as we now have for the maritimes in order to protect the province of Saskatchewan and one or two

other provinces against further loss of representation. You may feel, Mr. Chairman, that this is outside the scope of this legislation so I will not go into the matter further. However, it seems to me that this is as important an aspect of electioneering as the Canada Elections Act itself.
The hon. member for Skeena indicated that the changes mooted so far as advance polls are concerned are ones that he found quite agreeable. While the experience in Ontario has been a fairly expensive one in terms of the use made of advance polls by people voting in advance of the regular election day, and I would imagine that the per capita cost of such votes is very high, the fact that the service has been available has been very much appreciated. This provision is something about which we are quite enthusiastic.
I should also like to put forward our view that the fairest kind of arrangement for elections is the use of a permanent register. In that way you can hold an election much more quickly and have a shorter campaign. That is something the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate did not go into.

Mr. Chairman, I was privileged to be a member of the privileges and elections committee which considered the Canada Elections Act and the Canadian forces voting

regulations in their entirety. I was quite pleased with the manner in which the committee was conducted and I should like to pay my respects to the chairman of the committee, the hon. member for Queens, in addition to those which have already been expressed. I found something unusual in this committee. There was a great degree of harmony and attempts to come to fair conclusions in connection with all the sections that were considered. In a good many instances in which amendments were proposed to sections of the act, it was not unusual to find a member of one party moving the amendment and a member of another party seconding it, and then having it passed with unanimous approval.
As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate has stated, there were some cases in which differences of opinion arose. These were usually resolved and, in my opinion, the committee served a very useful function. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate stated that he felt the proposals amounted to no more than a tinkering with the act. I feel that the proposals amount to more than that. The committee dealt with each section of the act and a good deal of consideration was given to each section. There were many amendments made. I do not know, offhand, how many sections were amended, but I believe that approximately 50 sections were amended as well as many of the schedules. If the act, as amended in committee, is brought forward now it will be a much more workable act, and I hope that it will meet with the approval of all hon. members.
There are just two things I should like to mention about which I was quite pleased. The first one is the proposal for advance polls. This has been a difficult subject for a good many years. The proposed amendment would extend the advance poll so that anyone who expected to be out of his usual polling division on polling day would be able to vote, if the recommendation introduced by the committee is accepted. There were some amendments suggested which made the provisions for advance polls more acceptable than those in the act. It was recommended that advance polls be held on the Saturday and Monday, the ninth and seventh days respectively before polling day. I think this is an excellent proposal. The Saturday is a day on which a good many people who travel during the week are home, and on that occasion they would be able to vote. The following Monday is a day on which those people who are at their normal place of residence, but who may be away the following week, will be able to vote at an advance poll. I feel

that these two days are most satisfactory. They are sufficiently in advance of polling day that the returning officer will be able to exchange with deputy returning officers the names of the persons who voted at advance polls, thus preventing any attempt on the part of any person to vote twice.
The other provision with which I was particularly pleased concerned the appointment of revising agents in urban polls. There have been many complaints in years past about people being left off the list, in fact whole apartment buildings which may have been the starting point between two groups of enumerators and whole sections of streets have been omitted in some cases. In so far as the rural polls are concerned, it is very easy for a voter who has been left off the list to be sworn in on voting day. However, as we all know, if a mistake in an urban poll were not discovered until polling day the voter would have no vote. The provision for revising agents will certainly be a measure to prevent a situation of that kind arising.
The standing committee went into this whole matter carefully and I do not wish to take any more of the time of this committee. I feel the bill, as it will be introduced, embodying the main recommendations of the committee, will be acceptable to the members of the house.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few words to say on this resolution. All members of this house agree that the elections act should be enforced in such a way that franchise is respected and freely exercised.
I wholeheartedly support the proposed amendment to the act in order that the smallest possible number of people be disfranchised.
There is nevertheless a point I wish to emphasize, and I refer to the difference between the federal elections act and the provincial act. They are opposed to each other.
Here is a proof of this. Under the federal act, deputy returning officers have to initial each and every ballot at the very start, even before the voting takes place.
On the other hand, in the provinces-or perhaps should I say in the province of Quebec-ballots have to be initialed as each voter comes along and is recognized as being entitled to vote.
Those two methods are bound to be confusing. That is why I ask if it would not be possible for the chief electoral officer to come to an agreement in this regard with the various electoral officers of the provinces, for the sake of uniformity.
Canada Elections Act
Once again, under one system, the ballots are initialed at the beginning, while under the other, they are initialed as the voting takes place. Hence the confusion which sometimes occurs.
When an election takes place the polling box attendants receive instructions. Under the federal act, they are told that the ballots must be initialed before the beginning of the vote.
On the other hand, under the provincial act, the opposite is done.
The difficulty can even extend to the counting of the ballots. In fact, under the federal act, once the polls are closed, a deputy returning officer who failed to initial a ballot may do so, provided he does not see for whom the ballot has been cast.
In Quebec the returning officer is strictly prohibited from initialing a ballot he had forgotten to initial earlier.
The difference is therefore substantial and creates confusion. But where there is a risk of even greater confusion is when a federal election is held, say in April, followed by a provincial election a month later.
Let us suppose for a moment that the political parties hire the same election officers, the same partisans or else the most experienced ones. I realize that they are given instructions, but while such agents are fairly well educated, being usually chosen among people best able to understand the act, they must nevertheless be rather astonished to be told at one point: "You must initial every ballot before the vote" and then a month later: "You must not initial ballots in advance, you must initial them as the vote goes on."
Furthermore, in the first case, deputy returning officers are told: "If you have forgotten to initial a ballot, you may initial it provided that you do not see in whose favour the ballot has been cast.
On the other hand, it is the opposite in provincial elections.
For all those reasons, I think there is an urgent need for uniformity. I therefore suggest that the chief electoral officer in Ottawa get in touch with the various provincial electoral officers and that, after considering the matter they reach an agreement. It is of little consequence whether the federal or the provincial system prevails, so long as there is agreement.
Those are two cases I wanted to point out, Mr. Chairman. I think this type of amendment should promote the orderly conduct of elections.
613D

Canada Elections Act
Mention was made a moment ago of representatives. Here again, there is a change with regard to representatives.
Under the federal legislation, a candidate is entitled to two representatives, whereas in a provincial election, he can only have one. This too is a bit confusing. In fact under provincial legislation, if a candidate is found to have been represented at a poll by two representatives, not only must one of them get out, but he is liable to a fine. I think this has happened recently and that the second representative had to pay a fine.
I submit that, there too, we should have some uniformity in order to avoid confusion.
A few moments ago, reference was made to enumerators. I cannot see why, even if it would cost a bit more, we should not have two enumerators throughout the country, especially in small municipalities. I would not say that it necessarily happens in rural ridings, but, today, with summer residences and work being carried on all over the country, when an enumerator has more freedom and is appointed by only one party, he is sometimes tempted to drive on and not come back to list some family whose political affiliations do not seem to coincide with his own. We are familar with single enumerators in the province of Quebec; needless to say, having been appointed by the government in power, and being on their own in a city of about a million people, they acted just about as they pleased. They would take down names, in good or bad faith. Some of those people, of course, are more zealous than others. Some even said:	"When I call
at a home-I shall not say of Liberal or Conservative affiliation-but when I call at a Conservative, let us say, or a Liberal home, I call only once, I do not knock very loudly, and I do not come back. That is so true that- just to illustrate the point-during the last provincial election, it was decided, in the city of Montreal, to appoint two enumerators instead of one. Now, in the riding of Laurier, for instance, where a single enumerator was appointed by the Union Nationale, it was noted that 9,000 people of Italian origin had been registered, whereas this year, with two enumerators-I don't know what happened- but instead of 9,000 there were only 3,500. That is why it is always important to have an enumerator on each side. I submit that this is the only way to do it, if you want the enumeration to be as honest as possible.
The important point, therefore, is not how much it will cost this country. Indeed, even if it were to cost a few million dollars, never would an amount of money be more equitably

distributed, because each of the few thousand additional enumerators needed would earn $25, $30 or $35, as the case may be. Consequently, I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that the two enumerator system should be adopted throughout the country.
I do not think it would impoverish the country too much. At all events, if such were the case, at least a few thousand families would have $25, $30 or $35 extra income. Therefore, I respectfully submit, Mr. Chairman, that this system of two enumerators should apply throughout the country.
As far as representatives are concerned, last year I took up this matter with the predecessor of the secretary of state, the one whose services have been duly rewarded and who is now comfortably seated in the Senate. I do not bear him any grudge for it; I congratulate him. However, he had promised me then that certain parts of the act concerning the representatives would be amended.
At present, under the Canada Elections Act, a candidate may not hire more than one person for every 500 electors. In certain cases, this sets a limit of 90 on the number of persons a candidate may legally hire. Now it happens that, on election day, you have to muster from 200 to 400 representatives. Normally, under the act, those 200 or 400 representatives cannot be paid. Now, I do not think it is immoral, clandestine or irregular to pay someone who spends a whole day in a poll. At any rate, it cannot be claimed to be irregular to the point where it is punishable by a fine. Therefore, I submit that, in any discussion of amendments to the Canada Elections Act, there should be established a rate at which a candidate may pay his representatives at the polls. Another anomaly I wish to point out-and it is something that might have been done by the Liberals too- is the imposture which consists in getting persons bearing the same name as candidates to run against the latter, in order to take votes away from them. For instance, one Rene Levesque, an unknown artist, was a candidate in Laurier where the official Liberal candidate, who is very well known, had the same name. We went to the supposed address of that socalled Rene Levesque, and were told that there was no one there by that name. I think the law should be more strict in that regard, and that the returning officer should have greater responsibility with regard to the authenticity of various candidates bearing the same name. Such a stituation can have serious consequences. To give only one example, in

the constituency of Verdun, during the last election, a colleague, Mr. Yves Leduc, who was known to all here, was defeated by 1,700 votes, when his opponents brought in as a rival candidate a namesake who was completely unknown. Because the initials of the latter's given name came before those of Mr. Yves Leduc, his name was printed on the ballot before that of the official Liberal candidate. He got exactly 1,800 votes, that normally should have gone to Mr. Leduc, had it not been for that confusion which caused the Liberal candidate's defeat.
The same thing happened in Laurier where a certain Rene Levesque was made to run against the other. Fortunately, in this case, his name appeared after the name of Mr. Rene Levesque, the official Liberal candidate, and he didn't obtain enough votes to defeat the official candidate. But, Mr. Chairman, that famous Rene Levesque, of whom no one had ever heard before, who did not hold any meetings, managed all the same to get 900 votes by mistake. That is how some people claim to run honest elections and to be fair to all who have a right to vote. Bona fide candidates should be better protected under the act. For that purpose another amendment should be introduced.
In Quebec, the names of candidates representing the party in power and the opposition appear at the top of the ballot in alphabetical order, followed by the names of the other candidates, also in alphabetical order. The situation is different in regard to federal elections. I think amendments of this type should be considered, as they would help correct such abnormal and unfair situations.
It is a good thing that the name of that famous Rene Levesque, who was unknown in the constituency of Montreal-Laurier, appeared after the name of the official candidate; otherwise I think the unknown man might have been elected.

The Canada Elections Act should, to the greatest possible extent, be similar to the provincial elections legislation, or vice versa. I feel there should be an agreement between the provinces and the federal government in
Canada Elections Act
this regard. The matter should be considered at a federal-provincial conference, particularly in view of the fact that some provinces are now under premiers who are more willing than ever before to co-operate with Ottawa. Such an agreement would be helpful, and I think the matter should be raised at a federal-provincial conference, in order to solve that problem, to achieve uniformity in election laws, and to eliminate any danger of confusion in regard to the initials of candidates, party representatives, ballot counting, etc.

It would also be necessary to put a stop to terrorism exercised by goons cruising in automobiles, especially when it is known that police are part of such caravans. It is time, I am sure, to settle this problem.
I glanced at the proposed amendments to the Canada Elections Act, as regards the carrying of weapons. In the last election campaign, provincial police who were members of a political organization were seen carrying arms and moving about freely in the riding. Several of those policemen were in uniform; and those who were in plain clothes were carrying arms too, though, normally, they were not entitled to do so, since they were not electoral agents and the city police were affording citizens the normal protection.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Solicitor General to be good enough to consider those few suggestions, which we shall have an opportunity to bring up again when the different sections are examined.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I go along with the hon. members who have suggested that a great deal of good can flow from a conference between the chief electoral officer of Canada and the chief electoral officers of all the provinces. I think that if they met and drafted so far as is possible procedural regulations which would be acceptable to the various provinces as well as to the dominion it would be a wise and helpful

Canada Elections Act
thing in an attempt to obtain from an election that which a democratic election is intended to provide.
I find, and so does perhaps every hon. member of the house, most astonishing and disturbing news items appearing in the press concerning bold frauds which are being perpetrated during election time which are robbing people-and I use the word "robbing" with its fullest implications-of what I consider to be the most precious right and privilege which they have.
We have had prosecutions but I feel that the judiciary should perhaps regard these things a little more seriously than they do. Without mentioning a specific name there was the case of one man who was found guilty of having committed almost every offence against the elections act. He was guilty of every election practice of a corrupt nature. He pleaded guilty to the offences after a judicial inquiry presided over by one of the most eminent jurists in the province of Quebec and was ordered to be prosecuted. He was prosecuted and certainly one would have expected that for those offences he would have been sent to the penitentiary for at least five years. How shocking and disturbing it was that when he came before the magistrate he was sentenced to 30 days.
To me that was an act which did not discourage corrupt election practices but which treated them very lightly. I think our judiciary ought to be told that the theft of a vote is certainly as serious as the theft of vast sums of money, because vast sums of money sometimes are not as precious as the right to vote. I think we are all unanimous about the fact that the House of Commons is deeply concerned with seeing that these corrupt practices are stopped, particularly those which make it possible for one man to walk into a poll and say "I am Mr. Jones" when in fact he is not Mr. Jones. That is an impersonation which unfortunately is heard of during election times.
I want to suggest to the committee, and this is not a new suggestion but I think we should look at it more seriously than we have in the past, that we should have some means of identification by which a voter can walk into a poll and present his certificate of identification to the returning officer and say "Here is my certificate of identification and this is my photograph on it". Mr. Chairman, I hold in my hand a miniature certificate of naturalization which is my identity card anywhere in this country or elsewhere. It is perhaps the proudest possession I have and I say that no one can challenge me if

I walk into a poll, lay down my naturalization certificate with my photograph on it, and say "This is my identification; give me my ballot".
Of course, it can be done either with a birth certificate or with a simple certificate of identity which I suggest every voter should be armed with. If we can introduce that I say that there will be absolute certainty that there will be no impersonations at the polls.
I would like to pay tribute to two gentlemen of the cloth in the province of Quebec, Abbe Dion and Abbe O'Neil, who have virtually launched a crusade not only for the province of Quebec but for the whole of Canada and every municipality or where anyone has a right to vote for the elimination of corrupt practices. I think the House of Commons and its members should likewise form part of that crusade.
It is the most valuable thing we have, and if we evade or avoid this issue I do not think we are doing our duty as citizens or as legislators. I have heard some opposition to the suggestion that certificates of identity should be provided. As to the mechanics of the thing, I imagine it could be arranged without too much difficulty that six months, say, before an eleotion, citizens having the right to vote should go and obtain a certificate of identity. That would certainly not be as expensive as an enumeration. I have heard opposition expressed to the provision of certificates of identity with photographs attached to them on the grounds that this would make Canada into a police state. In what way? I have in the past regarded, and I would at this moment regard with grave suspicion anyone who believes that voters should not have a certificate with their photograph on them for presentation at the polls. What could be the purpose of opposing such a clear-cut method of identification? It would lead to our having the cleanest and finest expression of opinion by voters that it is possible to have.
I do not want to deal with all the unfortunate things which have happened in connection with elections, but can hon. members imagine the possibility that while the ballots are being counted someone should be able to walk off with a handful of ballots in his possession, to walk off and disappear. I think that is disgraceful. It is robbing the people and it is robbing the country of basic democratic rights, yet such offences are not treated as seriously as they should be. I think the theft of a ballot box, for example, should be regarded with extreme seriousness; the thief should be tracked down by the police or by officials and punished, when apprehended, with extreme rigour.

Speaking generally, it is possible that in rural areas that certificates of identity may not be so urgently needed, because there, I am told, the returning officer, the poll clerks and the scrutineers know the voters personally. That may be so, though I have no personal experience of elections in rural areas. However, in the urban centres it is not possible to know the voters personally. The secretary of state has access to his colleagues in the cabinet and I hope he will recommend to them that a system of certificates with photographs should be introduced at least in the urban centres.
That would reduce much of the hooliganism which we hear about and which is now a disgrace to our elections. I think such behaviour is a blot on the escutcheon of decency for which our country is noted. I do not want to recite the frightful things that happen in elections. To my mind such incidents are a disgraceful blot on our reputation and I urge the secretary of state to do everything in his power to see that they are eliminated. I defy anyone to tell me of a better means of identifying a voter when he comes into the poll than by providing him with a certificate containing his photograph properly sealed. This certificate of naturalization which I hold in my hand is perhaps the most precious thing I have. I am proud, too, that this happens to be signed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate. This is something that any man would be proud to possess, and certainly any Canadian who walks into a poll in order to exercise his rights to the franchise should be armed with a certificate of identity issued by the chief returning officer.

Mr. Chairman, may I add just a few words to what has just been said. I would like, in particular, to make some remarks following the suggestions made by the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis). In fact they seemed so sensible that I had trouble recognizing the hon. member. But, when he later gave instances of what had happened in some constituencies, he took the opportunity of playing politics to some extent and then I saw him under his true colours.
However, his suggestions are designed to prevent recurrence of certain things that happened in the last provincial election, not only in the constituency of Laurier, but also in another constituency where there was a Union Nationale candidate named McDuff. Well, there too an opponent also named McDuff was found and nominated. It is to
Canada Elections Act
avoid the repetition of similar incidents that the hon. member for St. Denis made his suggestion. Therefore, I, in turn would like to make a similar suggestion. We could adopt a measure which would change the present procedure to some extent, and instead of placing at the top of the ballot the name of the government candidate followed by that of the official opposition candidate, we would place at the top of the list the names of the candidates of parties which had representatives in the House of Commons during the last parliament, including those of C.C.F. representatives. In addition, to avoid fraud-for fraud is not restricted to one party only-I would put all those names in alphabetical order. I believe this would eliminate many unpleasant incidents.
The hon. member for St. Denis also said a moment ago that he had found a man named Rene Levesque, had gone to his home and, in short, had tried very hard to find that man. This identification would therefore eliminate all such confusion.
There might be another suggestion that I could make, because I agree also to what was said by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). In the province of Quebec a form that looks like an invoice is handed to us at the time of the enumeration. It seems extraordinary that one should be able to walk into a poll and vote without producing that form.
I think that the suggestion of the hon. member for Cartier makes a lot of sense. No doubt, it would come very handy on election day because it would eliminate impersonations or attempted impersonations and it would be very handy for everyone.
I think that the secretary of state should make a note of those suggestions for the next election. I believe they would be of tremendous help to the returning officers and the deputy returning officers, and especially for those who, having to cast their votes late in the day, arrive at the poll and find that somebody else voted in their place.
In my opinion, the main purpose of this resolution is making it easier for someone to vote who cannot do so on election day. Mr. Chairman, I may say that at the last election, I met many people who were finding it physically impossible to go out and vote. Now, it is a sacred right to vote; I would even add that it is our most important right and that we must protect it more and more. That is why we should take the proper steps so that every one may exercise that right.

Canada Elections Act
In closing, I should like to congratulate the secretary of state for introducing this piece of legislation. Furthermore, I must add that there has been no parliament which, at one time or another, did not have to amend the Canada Elections Act. In fact, the act has to be reviewed in the light of experience and of our developing population, and even in relation to new centres, because it is becoming more and more difficult for certain people in the newer communities to exercise their franchise. In short, the act should be periodically revised.
I am of the opinion that, as long as parliament considers the right to vote as most important, all the citizens will be guaranteed greater freedom.
In closing, I should like to insist on the proposition put forward by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). Mr. Chairman, I frankly confess that I doubt if it was necessary to make such a suggestion. I feel this should have been done long ago. Who would suffer any harm if, in a country like Canada, election briefs were printed in both languages?
We are always eager to point out in our speeches that Canada is a bilingual country, and that it is necessary to achieve national unity. But when the time comes for concrete action, there are always some who refuse to go along.
Had I merely supported and seconded the suggestion of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm I feel I would not have wasted my time.
I ask the secretary of state to look carefully into that suggestion so that those antiquated views that are uncalled for today may be put aside.
Let us take a step forward, however small it may be, toward national unity of all groups, not only of two races, but of all those that form our country. Let us publish election briefs in both official languages.

maintopic: REPORTED BAN ON FAREWELLS TO CREWS OF NORTHERN SUPPLY SHIPS
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING CONSOLIDATION, ADVANCE POLLS, ADMINISTRATION, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had the pleasure of being a member of the committee which studied the Canada Elections Act and I may say, like the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), that the committee functioned very well. Our suggestions were not all accepted, but just the same, the committee did an excellent job, so that all of us who were on it were convinced that, even if we did not fully agree, all of us sincerely wished to make elections easier for the voters and as honest as possible.

Our remarks were not made in a critical vein and there was no feeling of bitterness, even when someone did not see eye to eye with us.
However, I believe that we must further insist on certain changes being made.
First, I take the suggestion of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), which was taken up by the hon. member for Mont-magny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin).
That suggestion was not discussed with acrimony. Someone said that he did not see the necessity of having briefs in both languages. There was no malice on the part of the members who were opposed to it. Someone simply expressed this view: If it is not necessary to do so, why do it?
As the hon. member for Montmagny-L'lslet pointed out, I say it is time we proved that we have achieved a certain degree of maturity and that is by practising bilingualism that we will show that the whole of Canada is the business of the federal government.
I take up the argument of the member for Montmagny-L'Islet: What harm would it do to anyone to have election briefs issued in both languages?
Those who cannot read French can read English, and vice versa.
The same applies to bilingual cheques. They would be good even if they were printed in both languages. That proposal could be accepted throughout the country. That is how nationalism develops. There is certainly nothing dangerous in having both on the same piece of paper.
Were it only to emphasize that suggestion of the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet, I think I was justified in rising to support that proposal.
Let us forget the old tags like: "We must not talk French there, otherwise we will get crucified: we must not talk English there, otherwise we will get crucified."
It is time Quebec people knew that English is one of the two official languages in this country; and that people in the other provinces realized that French is one of the official languages in Canada.
In short, I wholeheartedly support the suggestion. Unfortunately we were unable to get action on it. Perhaps the acting minister will convince his colleagues that such action would be a good thing.
Anyhow, there is no reason for despair. Canada is developing over the years. In the

life of a nation, ten, 15 or 20 years are little enough, even if they represent a long time in the life of man.
By submitting the same suggestions over and over again, the day will come when all the people, knowing one another better, will And out that the suggestions were justified.
I shall make a digression and tell the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis) that one of his suggestions at least has been accepted.
Formerly, a candidate was entitled to one representative for each 500 voters. Now we can employ the number of persons reasonably required to represent the interests of a candidate during an election. Of course, those people will have to be compensated.
There has been reference to the initialing of ballots. As previously pointed out I think it is important that ballots be initialed as suggested.
An election took place recently in Quebec. There were some ballots which had obviously been initialed during the day, but at different hours and in different ways. Consequently, the judges found it extremely difficult to decide whether those ballots should be rejected or not.
The suggestion made earlier should be carried out: A few minutes before the polls open, the representatives of the various candidates should see to it that all ballots are initialed right at the start.
Mistakes occasionally happen. For instance, a scrutineer will inadvertently pick up two ballots at a time. At the end of the day, one lacks a signature. What is to be done?
With regard to this matter the federal legislation is good, and allows that lapse to be corrected. Anyhow, I think that the federal act is superior to the provincial legislation in this field. When I speak of the provincial legislation, I obviously mean the Quebec laws, because they are the only ones with which I am familiar, apart from the Canada Elections Act. On the other hand, the provincial elections act is better than the federal legislation with regard to the appointment of the deputy returning officer and the poll clerk.
According to federal law, the appointment of the deputy returning officer and of the clerk is made by the returning officer. That responsibility, which is imposed upon him often gives rise to criticism. There are candidates who express wishes, or have whims, and who, when they are not satisfied, are harshly critical.
It can also happen that the returning officer is more friendly towards this or that person.
79951-0-387
Canada Elections Act
Personal feeling may come into play. In other words, as it is, the Canada Elections Act, on this particular point, is deficient.
Let us follow the Quebec act. It is clear and easy to apply.
I think the minister might listen to my suggestion, and resume his conversation later with the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell).
Here is my suggestion. I was saying that the Quebec act, in this field, is superior to the federal act. There is no danger of errors being made. Even the returning officer, conscious of doing his duty, is sometimes subject to criticism. He is given considerable responsibility, which he would no doubt like to avoid.
Returning officers would rather not have to appoint deputy returning officers or poll employees.
Now here is what the Quebec act says in section 171, about the persons to be appointed in each voting section of the whole electoral district:
The returning officer shall appoint as scrutineer the person recommended therefor by the government candidate, and as poll clerk the person recommended therefor by the candidate of the opposition party.
We could probably change this formula as follows: the scrutineer would be appointed by the candidate having polled the most votes at the last election; and the poll clerk by the candidate having polled the second heaviest vote at the last election.
So would the act decree. We would thus know beforehand who would be appointing the deputy returning officer, and who would appoint the poll clerk. This would at the same time eliminate malevolent criticism directed against the returning officer.
The recommendations would be made by the Prime Minister to the returning officer, and by the Leader of the Opposition, who would recognize their representative by means of letters.
So, I suggest that section 26 of the Canada Elections Act be replaced by section 171 of the Quebec act. That would do the trick.
I recall that, at the committee, an hon. member said that such procedure introduced politics in the electoral field. Now, now, let us come to some agreement-
If the person is appointed according to the provisions of the act, we avoid the delicate situation in which only one party would be represented at the poll.
The suggestion has even more weight when the polling takes place in remote communities.
Today, Indians have the right to vote. In some cases they may have to travel distances up to 100 miles in order to cast their ballots.

Canada Elections Act
I know, lor instance, that the member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) has some polls at 100 or even 300 miles from population centres. If a representative has to be sent by plane or helicopter, it adds substantially to the cost of the election. However, there is a continuing demand for lower election costs.
If, as I suggest, there were for instance a representative of the Conservative party and of the C.C.F. party, both would have a representative, and there would be no danger of any fraud.
Sometimes, a representative may be overly enthusiastic without being dishonest. He may do things that are not entirely commendable. My suggestion would help him in the discharge of his duties.
I made the same point in the committee, and I would ask the secretary of state to suggest to his colleagues that the provision I have quoted from section 171 of the Quebec elections act be substituted for section 26 of the federal elections act. That, I think, would be a substantial improvement.
Reference was made to election costs. In my view, they are too heavy. However, the point is rather delicate. In such cases, if there are too many restrictions, the results are just opposite of what was expertion.
I remember a few years ago that the Hon. Mr. Powers, then a private member of the house and now a senator, was looking for a way to improve the act insofar as election expenses were concerned. He thought expenses were too high and tried to remedy the situation.
What happened? In some ridings, people disregarded the act, and money was spent as though nothing had happened.
Personally, I should like the act to be strictly and honestly enforced.
I think there are certain provisions in our statutes which only confuse things and for which we have no need. What is the use of keeping useless provisions in force?
A word about the identity card. It has been a long time since that card was abolished; it was issued to us during the last war, as a war measure. I think it could be of great service in peacetime. It would be a help to very honest citizen in Canada. It would include his name, address and photograph.
I might quote an example to show its usefulness. Suppose you want to cross the American border. There is no need for a passport. All you need is an identity card which you carry in your wallet. It saves time and gets you across the border without trouble.

At election time, it could prove most useful. At this point, I agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl)-who is himself an immigrant and therefore holds a Canadian citizenship card -that native Canadians also be provided with a similar card.
It would also be useful in places where people under 21 or under 16 are not allowed, because that card would show the date of birth. It would therefore be easy to establish whether there is voluntary or involuntary error.
Mr. Chairman, I think that, on the whole, the Canada Elections Act is not _ bad. But many changes could be made which would enable us to improve it.
It might be appropriate to take that part of the Quebec elections act which stipulates that the enumerator shall be selected by the party in office or by the group which polled most votes at the last election, while the group which received the second highest number of votes shall appoint the second enumerator. Thus, the act would be almost perfect and I know that everybody in this country would benefit by it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about the election act committee. I was a member of the committee and spent much time at its meetings. I thought the committee did a very good job. We had a wonderful chairman, and thank heaven that the last speaker and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate were not allowed full play. We had a very good representation on the committee.
There is one other thing I wish to say with respect to getting the vote out in rural areas. At Dawson Creek the junior chamber of commerce got people out to vote and the only bloomer made was made by the returning officer or a deputy returning officer. Seven hundred people were left off the voters' list, and this man had been appointed by the Liberal government. I think the committee did a wonderful job thanks to my colleague who was there to look after things. That is all I have to say.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to delay the passage of the resolution but I should like to add something to what has been said by the hon. member for St. Denis, not with respect to provincial but rather federal elections and with relation to my own constituency of Laurier. I feel that the committee should have some knowledge of what transpired in that constituency in

1957, and I believe I can impart that information in just a few moments. I think it would be of interest to the committee to know some of the things that took place so that the committee could take into consideration the suggestions that have beeen made from time to time by those who are responsible for the holding of such elections, as well as by the committee itself. I am glad that the secretary of state is in his seat and responsible for this measure, because I am sure that when he listens to what I have to put on the record he will be as surprised as many of us were when these incidents took place.
I hold in my hand now the report of the returning officer for the electoral district of Laurier for the federal election of 1957. I am only going to read three or four paragraphs from this report to bring them to the attention of the committee. I will not read all of it because it would be too lengthy. It begins this way:
(Translation):
The moment the polls opened, 225 ballots were stolen from poll No. 82 (at 482V Henrl-Jullen). I immediately advised the R.C.M.P. and went on the spot to investigate and replace the stolen ballots.
Soon after the theft at poll 82, 275 ballots were stolen from poll 62 located at 4730 Delaroche street. The R.C.M.P. was immediately advised and the municipal police were already on the spot to investigate. I gave new ballots to the deputy returning officer.
Around 11 a.m., at poll 103 (located at 5210 Chambord street) goons stuffed into the ballot box some papers looking like ballots. Eye-witnesses took down the licence number of the car used by the intruders for their getaway.
From 11 a.m. until closing time (7 p.m.), from all parts of Laurier riding came complaints and requests for help from deputy returning officers who were being threatened, annoyed, molested and even injured by goons who forced papers looking like ballots into ballot boxes and took advantage of their visit to steal ballots from the desk of poll officers.
Early in the afternoon, at poll 58 (located at 4600 Boyer street), the deputy returning officer managed to snatch from the hands of an intruder who was trying to stuff them into the box a bundle of those papers which had been circulating from poll to poll since the opening of the polls.
The deputy returning officer handed me those papers. They were ballots, twenty of them; at first sight they looked like genuine ballots.
After close inspection, with the help of two experts, I can state that they were counterfeit ballots.
(Text):
There were hundreds of false ballots that circulated in the constituency. I saw them. I have no right to have them in my possession, and they were turned over to the chief electoral officer, but the situation continued during the whole of that day.
Here is the last but one sentence of consequence in the report, and it states:
79951-0-387J
Canada Elections Act (Translation):
I have reason to believe that at least half the polls in the electoral district of Laurier were visited by election thieves.
Moreover, I am advising them that a large number of counterfeit ballots are circulating in the Laurier electoral district.
(Text):
More than that, in one constituency there were two gentlemen who entered with pistols in their hands, lined up four people in the poll against the wall and did succeed in taking the box from the poll. It was afterwards recovered. I am happy to say that thanks to the efforts of the chief electoral officer these incidents were not repeated in 1958. All I want to do is to bring to the attention of the minister the recommendation which was made by the returning officer, and it is contained in this short paragraph:
(Translation):
In closing, I should like to point out that we have great difficulty in getting people to act as deputy returning officer or clerk.
In the face of such a situation, I think it would be advisable to group the polls in schools or public halls.
In that way, there could be 8, 10 or 12 polls under the supervision of a police officer.
Thus election thieves could not take advantage of a woman's physical weakness to commit their crimes.
(Text):
I know that while that is an excellent recommendation, namely that in those areas where there have been difficulties and assaults consideration should be given to putting a number of polls, eight, ten or twelve as is suggested, in schools, I realize to do that one must obtain permission of the school board and that is not always an easy matter. I do feel consideration should be given to this matter because it is something which the committee, the house, the minister and all the members of parliament would not want to see repeated either in this particular constituency or in any other constituency.
I may add that because of the manner in which the returning officer in the constituency of Laurier conducted himself he was afterwards assaulted on the streets of the city of Montreal while returning from a medical call. He is a doctor. He had to spend more than a month in the hospital and it took months and months before the culprit was apprehended. I do hope, therefore, the minister will be able to give consideration to these suggestions. I am sure, too, that the chief electoral officer has the matter well in hand and has made recommendations, not only to the committee but to the minister, which I trust will be given consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I also would like to make a few remarks regarding unfortunate incidents which happened in my constituency during the general election of 1957 and, like the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier), I would ask the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer), to take the necessary steps to avoid repetition of similar incidents.
On June 10, 1957, election day, a few thugs from Montreal who had been hired by my opponent, came to a poll and pushed the poll officers against the wall, with the result that when the ballots were counted at night it was found that those gentlemen had made a mistake: instead of using an ordinary lead pencil to mark the ballots they had used a ball-point pen, so that all those ballots, which had been marked for my opponent, were cancelled.
Mr. Chairman, I ask the Solicitor General to make the provisions of the

elections act strict enough to prevent the repetition of similar situations, for in a parish like Ste. Helene de Bagot, where all the people know one another, such incidents cause much flurry and fear among the people and this does not help promote a favourable view of our elections in Canada.
Like the hon. member for Laurier, I urge the Solicitor General to see that such incidents do not happen again.

I just rise to commend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate particularly on one point, namely that perhaps the secretary of state even yet could have another look at the suggestion that deputy returning officers and poll clerks could be selected in a manner similar to that in which we select enumerators in urban polls, where one is selected by one party representative and one by the other.
Reference was made to my constituency as being one of half a dozen or so that embrace a great deal of territory. As a result of other amendments that are being made to the act and as to which I do not want to make a detailed explanation, the committee will recognize that a number of locations where polls have not been set up in the past will now require polls. I can think of perhaps a dozen such polls that will now be necessary but that have not been necessary in federal elections in the past in the constituency of Kenora-Rainy River. They are similar to the one used for purposes of illustration by the hon. member for Port Arthur. They can be reached only by aeroplane and frequently only by chartered aeroplane. In consequence, hon. members will realize that it is simply out of the question for candidates to send in their representatives to such polls.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate indicated that he thought this form of poll operation should be applied to rural polls. That procedure, of course, would be a fine thing in itself. However, I differ with my hon. friend in this respect. I have examined the records of the proceedings of previous house committees examining the elections act and I find that the distinguished members of the Conservative party who in those days made these recommendations were for the most part representatives of urban ridings. I think this suggestion should appeal equally to members from urban ridings.
If this system were adopted I think we would find that in the near future we would

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to express my thanks to the hon. member for Davenport who the other evening was good enough to suggest that the bill be held up until I had an opportunity of expressing my opinion on it and discussing it. I do not want to do that other than briefly. I want to reiterate what was expressed by our side of the house in the first instance, that because this is a bill which will develop the natural resources, not only of the province of Newfoundland but also of the province of Quebec, we favour the bill now as we did formerly.
There are, however, in view of the evidence which was given before both the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines as well as a similar committee in the other house, some observations which I would ask the committee to listen to and to bear with me as I bring them before it.
The first which comes to my mind is that the Wabush-Carol (Agreement) act, 1959, which is set out in the preamble to Bill No. S-24, and again in clause 3 of the bill, provides for the Northern Land Company to grant to the Wabush running rights in perpetuity. This is found in section 3 of the Wabush railway and the Carol agreement granting the running rights in perpetuity.

This is found in section 3 of the Wabush-Carol (Agreement) act, 1959, which I would like to put on record. It reads:
Land company will grant to Wabush railway and to Carol company, respectively, in perpetuity,
(a)	the right to run trains and otherwise to operate the railway over, maintain and make connections with the tracks and facilities to be constructed by Land company on the joint section in accordance with clause 2 (the tracks and facilities to be constructed by Land company in, on and over the joint sections being hereinafter called the "joint facilities''), provided, however, that except by agreement with Land company, neither Wabush railway nor Carol company may use the joint facilities to an extent greater than fifty per centum of the capacity thereof, and provided further that such use shall be upon the payment of an equitable share of all expenses, depreciation, taxes and other charges applicable to the joint facilities and the joint section; and
(b)	the right to use and enjoy such rights, benefits and privileges granted to Land company under clause 1 and to use any additional lands conveyed or agreed to be conveyed to Land company by reason of the railway grant as may be reasonably necessary for the operation of a railway over the joint facilities or otherwise, provided, however, that neither Wabush railway nor Carol company shall construct stations, freight sheds, sidings or other railway facilities on the joint section or on said additional lands where the same would interfere unreasonably with the constructions and operation of the joint facilities.
Section 10 of the Wabush-Carol (Agreement) act refers to agreements contemplated by the act and prohibits any assignment or transfer without the consent of all parties. It is a short section and perhaps I may be allowed to put it on the record:
This agreement and any agreement contemplated hereby-
And I lay stress on the word "contemplated".
-shall not be assigned by Wabush railway, Land company and Carol company, or by any of them, in whole or in part, except pursuant to an agreement or agreements by and between the said companies and which said agreement or agreements may on the terms and conditions therein specified permit an assignment, in whole or in part. An assignment or proposed assignment or other transfer of this agreement or the rights hereunder, in whole or in part, in violation of this clause shall be void and of no force and effect.
It is common ground following what I have put on record that the running rights agreements contemplated by the Wabush-Carol (Agreement) act have not yet been signed, as the hon. sponsor knows and also most of those who listened to the evidence in the committee. They are now in the process of negotiation. At page 1355 of the report of the proceedings before the house committee on June 28, 1960, Mr. Pattillo is quoted as saying this in reply to my question:

maintopic: REPORTED BAN ON FAREWELLS TO CREWS OF NORTHERN SUPPLY SHIPS

speechtext: Have you completed all of your agreements with the Carol Lake Railway Company?

subtopic: WABUSH LAKE RAILWAY COMPANY AND ARNAUD RAILWAY COMPANY
speechtext:
No, we have not, Mr. Chevrier. We have had what I call, for lack of a better phrase,

a letter of intent. Some of the agreements contemplated by that letter of intent have been made; some have not yet been completed. But they will have to be a matter for negotiation in the future. But I cannot see how what we are seeking here in any way affects that.
The situation, therefore, at the present time, is that the Carol Lake company, which will remain under Newfoundland jurisdiction, will enter into an agreement with Northern Land Company for running rights in perpetuity, which agreement will include both the rights to Carol Lake company and the obligations of Carol Lake company.
Wabush Lake Railway Company, if the bill under consideration is enacted, might enter into a similar agreement, but the question would then arise as to possible conflict between clause 3 and clause 5 of the bill, and as to whether the provisions of the Newfoundland statute or of the Railway Act would apply. Under the Wabush-Carol (Agreement) act the running rights agreements would be in perpetuity. If the Railway Act applies, section 156, subsection 2 of that act would limit any such agreement to 21 years.
The proponents of this bill have consistently taken the position that, other than to secure the right to have rates fixed by the board of transport commissioners, they do not want in any way to change the picture that exists between the two companies authorized to enter into an agreement by the Wabush-Carol (Agreement) act, and they have so stated repeatedly not only in the house committee but in the committee of the other place.
Again I should like to quote from the report of the proceedings before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines of June 28, 1960. Mr. Pattillo, speaking on behalf of the proponents of the legislation, made the following statement as reported at page 1354;
We have examined the thing very carefully. We have studied all the documents in existence between the Iron Ore Corporation and ourselves. We know of no contractual obligation that is affected by the bill. But we are not the least adverse to giving this protection, and accordingly section 6 has been put in there. We do not want in any way to change the picture that exists between us except to give us the power, which they presently have, of going to the board of transport commissioners.
So it would appear that the main question in so far as the proponents of this bill are concerned is the tariff. On that there can be no disagreement. I think they are certainly within their rights in wanting to go before the board for that purpose. The same statement as I have quoted here from Mr. Pattillo was made on several occasions before the Senate and the Senate committee. I should like, if I may, to put on record what was
Private Bills
said in that committee by the Hon. Mr. Brunt, which can be found at page 724 of the proceedings, dated Tuesday, May 31, 1960:
May I point out to hon. senators that counsel for the two railways applying for the passing of this bill said in their statements that this was the furthest thing from their minds, and that if any contractual obligations actually existed at the time this bill was being passed there was no desire on their part to avoid any of them or to be relieved from carrying out all their contractual obligations. I think that nothing can be clearer than a statement which is to be found in the printed proceedings at page 68. This statement was made during the hearing which took place on May 12 by Mr. De Roche, one of the counsel appearing for the applicants, and it is as follows;
"We don't intend to be relieved of anything and we feel confident we have not relieved ourselves of anything."
So I say that the sponsors of this bill instantly consented to all the amendments which have been suggested, which would make it clear beyond the shadow of a doubt that they were not being relieved of any of their contractual obligations despite the act, and that they are liable for all their contractual obligations now existing, whether or not the bill is granted. The situation is, as I understand it, as follows, namely that the proponents of this bill have consistently taken the position that they do not wish to change the position that existed between the parties to agreements signed or contemplated other than to secure the right to have the rates fixed by the board of transport commissioners. Without going into the question of possible conflict between clauses 3 and 5 of the bill it would appear that the proponents would have no objection to the inclusion of an addition to clause 6 which I shall mention in a moment, which would only leave the parties in the situation in which they were prior to the adoption of the bill, and particularly as contemplated by the Wabush-Carol (Agreement) act and still leave the companies affected by the bill free to have their rates fixed by the board.
I said at the outset and I repeat now that here is a railway which extends some 350 miles or more, partly into the province of Newfoundland and partly into the province of Quebec, to each end of which there has been added a railway line, 40 miles in length at the north extremity and 20 miles or thereabouts in length at the southern extremity, and it seems to me that the chief concern of the proponents is to see to it that they are not unfairly treated in so far as the rate for moving their ore is concerned. They say they will be perfectly happy if they were placed within the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners so that the board could fix the rate. If the board fixed the rate they

Private Bills
would be perfectly happy even though it might be higher than the amount they thought it should be.
My only reason for rising at this time is to ask the sponsor of this bill if he would not, in view of what has been said by the proponents of this bill and their counsel both in the other place and in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, consent not only to protect the rights which have been consumated thus far but also to protect those that are in contemplation. Of course, the hon. sponsor will remember that Mr. Pattillo made it clear that clause 6 as it now stands can only apply to those agreements which have been completed and cannot apply to agreements that are in contemplation. So I ask the sponsor if he will not consent to amending clause 6, when we get to it, in order that it may read as follows:
Nothing in this act shall release either of the companies from any of its contractual obligations nor affect nor render inoperative the terms of any agreement contemplated by the provisions of the acts of the legislature of the province of Newfoundland referred to in the preamble.
If this were done I think there could certainly be no objection taken by those who opposed the bill in committee, and I now ask the page if he will give one of these copies to the clerk and one to the sponsor of the bill.
The Depuiy Chairman: I assume this will affect clause 6 when we reach it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make the following comment so that I can explain the position I must take. In respect to clause 5, the contention is that this clause is not meant in any way to permit the company to do that which it has agreed not to do, but merely gives the company a capacity that it might not otherwise have. I have not the evidence at hand, but Mr. Pattillo states that although clause 5 might apply and give this capacity the company will still be bound by the agreement made, in spite of clause 5. That leaves us, in effect, with the suggestion about agreements to be made and these are contained in what are known as letters of intent. The only reason they cannot legally be covered by the act is that the agreements have not advanced to a stage at which they could be called completed agreements.
I understand that in the discussions in the other place the sponsor of the bill made it clear that he was quite prepared at that time to make any changes which in the opinion
[Mr. Chevrier.I
of Mr. O'Brien, the counsel, would legally ensure these rights which the sponsor intends to carry out but no wording at that time could be devised that would have this effect. The same problem was discussed in the committee. Mr. Pattillo said he did not want to go on record as saying that they could legally be bound by the letter of intent but it was the consensus that they wished to negotiate and complete the agreement to the letter and thus follow their original intention. No wording could be arrived at to cover an agreement in intention. It is rather awkward to make such an amendment, as was found in the other place.
At this stage I feel that undue delay would result from this amendment. I understand that every possible combination was tried to satisfy Mr. O'Brien when the matter was before the other place. The other place experienced difficulty in trying to arrive at acceptable wording to an amendment that would cover the thing not actually brought into the contract.
There may be opinions-and Mr. Pattillo did not want to stand on that-that even the letter of intent could be used as a basis of enforcement and agreement under the circumstances. Neither Mr. Pattillo nor I want to leave the committee with the impression that this could be done. However, there is a legal basis there that should the company attempt a breach of the agreement the companies would be protected through the wording of the letter of intention and the expression of intention already demonstrated in the proceedings to date.
I feel that an amendment is not necessary under the circumstances. If one could have been found when the matter was before the other place I am sure it would have been approved at that time. The feeling of the group in the other place was that such wording was not necessary. We feel that the matter as it stands protects all the interests of the parties according to the original intention. I have no authority to agree to an amendment at this stage.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word on this. The hon. member

for Davenport has said that he does not feel the amendment proposed by my friend the hon. member for Laurier is necessary. It may be that it is not necessary. I do not think there is any particular point in arguing that. The fact is, however, that it certainly is not an amendment which could conceivably do the petitioners for this bill any harm if they are acting in good faith, because all it says is: -nor affect nor render inoperative the terms of any agreement contemplated by the provisions of the acts of the legislature of the province of Newfoundland referred to in the preamble.
It seems to me that in view of the fact that we are legislating about rights which without our legislation are rights within a province, we should be very careful to see that both parties affected are not inadvertently injured in any way. It is a principle of legislation which the hon. member's leader has often stressed-more often when the hon. gentleman was over here than he has more recently, I admit-that rights should not be left to good faith at all but should be nailed down in the statute beyond any shadow of doubt.
It is, after all, not a question of the petitioner's wishes in the matter. This bill, if it passes, will be a law of the parliament of Canada. It is for us in this chamber to exercise our own judgment about it. We should not consider ourselves as rubber stamps for any petitioner on either side. It seems to me that in the light of what my hon. friend has put forward as to the desirability of making sure that the undertakings the petitioners indicated they have every intention of carrying out will be carried out-and I do not doubt their goodwill in the matter at all; I am sure they intend to carry out these undertakings-and if we can give the matter an additional legal sanction we should do so.
I am not a lawyer but I listened very carefully to what my friend the hon. member for Laurier said. I feel that this amendment would appear to give additional protection in the matter. Since we are going to be here for some few days in any case and since it is perhaps desirable to give the hon. ladies and gentlemen in the other place employment part of the time, I cannot think that there would be any great difficulty about sending this back and asking for their concurrence in an amendment so obviously and palpably just as the amendment proposed by my hon. friend.
