speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, earlier in my remarks on second reading I explained the purpose of the amendment I will propose in relation to this clause. As it is now, the nomination of the deputy returning officer is the responsibility of the returning officer. In certain cases difficulties arise from this fact. In some instances the returning officer may be friendlier toward one candidate than he is toward the other and one candidate may be hated by the person who is the returning officer. This may result in an individual suffering from his decisions. Even if a returning officer acts according to the law and his oath of office he is always criticized because always one will not be satisfied with his decision.
Furthermore in remote districts it costs a large sum of money for candidates to send someone to represent them. Now that Indians will be voting we will have people voting in districts more remote than the districts where voting has taken place heretofore. If the candidate has to charter a plane or helicopter to send a man to supervise it will be extremely costly and it may mean an exorbitant expense for a candidate who is poorer than his rival candidate.
In the provisions governing elections in the province of Quebec we have an arrangement which has worked very well. In Quebec the deputy returning officer is nominated by the candidate of the government and the clerk is nominated by the opposition candidate. But in the federal parliament we have more than two parties and therefore under my proposal the deputy returning officer would be nominated by the candidate or the party which had the most votes at the previous election and the clerk would be recommended by the candidate or party with the second largest number of votes at the preceding election. In that way candidates would be able to rely on their own man to supervise in remote parts of ridings and would know that everything was all right.
There would always be representatives of at least two parties in the remote settlements and as a result everyone would be satisfied. It would ensure perfect safety to the candidates through the fact that there would be representatives of two parties there, whether a Conservative and a C.C.F. in certain regions,

a Liberal and a C.C.F. in another region or a Liberal and a Conservative in another region. There would always be two persons to supervise and to see that everything was done according to the law. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Levis, these two amendments to subclauses 1 and
4.	I move this amendment to subclause 1 of clause 26:
Such deputy returning officer be selected in the same manner as urban enumerators by the candidate who received the highest vote at the last preceding election.
To subclause 4 of clause 26 I move this amendment:
Such clerks be selected by the candidate who received the second highest vote at the last preceding election.

Mr. Chairman, first of all I must say it is really refreshing to hear from members on the other side of the house words

of praise for the Quebec elections act. For years and years we have been used to hearing them, especially the hon. member for Hull, trying to take the elections act of the province of Quebec to pieces. Of the ten provincial elections acts in Canada the hon. member for Hull is now using as support for his proposition the elections act of Quebec. I must say this is refreshing.
Unfortunately I think the hon. member is a little bit off the track with this amendment. He wants the public of Canada to pay for the electoral expenses of the candidates of the two large parties of Canada. That is precisely what his amendment means. His big argument is to plead for the candidates and he wants us to insert such an amendment in the act so that candidates will be able to save money at public expense because he thinks it is too expensive for candidates to send scrutineers or representatives to outlying areas.
Under the Canada Elections Act it has been decided very wisely that the deputy returning officers and the poll clerk shall both be election officers and as such they are the officers who are in charge of the application of the Canada Elections Act and the regulations under that act at the poll on the day of the election. For that purpose both of them have to be sworn in. The deputy returning officer has to take an oath which reads as follows:
I, the undersigned, appointed deputy returning officer for polling station No.-of the electoral district of-do swear (or solemnly affirm) that I am qualified as an elector in the said electoral district, that I will act faithfully in my said capacity of deputy returning officer, without partiality, fear, favour or affection, and that I will keep secret the name of the candidate for whom the ballot paper of any elector is marked in my presence at the pending election. So help me God.
The oath that the clerk takes is in the following words:
I, the undersigned, appointed poll clerk for the above mentioned polling station, do swear (or solemnly affirm) that I am qualified as an elector in the said electoral district, that I will act faithfully in my capacity of poll clerk, or in that of deputy returning officer, if required to act as such, without partiality, fear, favour or affection, and that I will keep secret the name of the candidate for whom the ballot paper of any elector is marked in my presence at the pending election. So help me God.
I think this indicates very clearly that these persons are both election officers and as such they are there to serve the public and not to serve a political party. They are not there to save money for candidates of any party. I think we can have confidence in the Canadians who are chosen to carry out such offices, and for my own part I believe, and I think the committee will agree, that any Canadian who takes such an oath
Canada Elections Act
will not try to show any partiality or anything like that and take it upon himself to carry out the instructions of the law and the regulations under the Canada Elections Act.

What my friend the hon. member for Hull was saying was that just as the appointment of the two enumerators in urban polls, one selected not by the two great parties-the Solicitor General misrepresented my hon. friend's amendment because it does not say that; the law in Quebec says that but not the amendment of the hon. member for Hull- the hon. member for Hull says exactly what the present Canada Elections Act says regarding enumerators, that is to say that the deputy returning officer would be selected by the candidate having the highest number of votes at the last previous election whether he was C.C.F., Liberal, Conservative, an independent or whatever he was, and the clerk would be selected by the person having the second highest number of votes regardless of the party to which he belonged.

As a matter of fact, we know that there are many polls in remote parts of this country where candidates cannot afford to send scrutineers because of the great cost; and we know what will happen if the deputy returning officer and the poll clerk are both appointed by the returning officer who is appointed by political patronage as everybody knows and always has been, and anybody who wants to pretend to the contrary is pretending and doing

nothing else. We know that there are suspicions in certain circumstances that these elections will not be conducted in the way we think they ought to be. Canada Elections Act
The second objection made by the Solicitor General is the question of pointing out that there will be no impartiality at the polls. There will be. Then there is this question of an oath. The Solicitor General has contended that because these two people take an oath they must be believed and we expect that they will be honourable in the discharge of their duties. But what is there to suggest that these other two people who take the same oath will not be honourable in the discharge of their duty? You can give both the same oath. This business of saying that the appointees at the polls are not interested politically is purely a fiction of politics, a fiction of law. The fact is that they are two Canadians, as the secretary of state points out. Give them the same oath. But what you are doing is that you are making it possible in the remote areas of the country where it is not possible to have scrutineers to have a sense of impartiality by having two representatives at the polls. speechtext: Perhaps I should rise and express my complete disapproval of this amendment. I am unalterably opposed to it. This is not a banana republic, even if the official opposition would apparently like to have it that way by this

He was not here this afternoon when the hon. member for St. Denis explained the situation and I think that probably all the members from the province of Quebec will agree with me that the

purpose of the amendment as explained by the hon. member for St. Denis was very clear. It was far from his mind to propose anything which was not democratic. I want to say to the hon. member for Assiniboia that the purpose was not to cast aside the C.C.F. party or any party, but to prevent confusion in the ballots. Once again, I say my hon. friend's only purpose was to avoid the confusion which is sometimes experienced, especially, as I say, in the province of Quebec where such incidents have happened in two or three elections-and I am not casting reflections on any party.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, far be it from us to wish to stop those phony names and phony candidates from coming in, because they will do so anyway. Now, I believe that a party which wants to use phony names or names of people who do not exist, will probably also have nomination papers signed, and that phony name will appear on the ballot. However, in that case, the party in power and the opposition party will at least have the privilege of having the names of their candidates placed on the ballot, which is not the case now under the federal act.
That was precisely what happened in Verdun-and I repeat what I said this afternoon-where a Mr. Leduc was the official candidate and a certain other Mr. Leduc was nominated, whose initial came before that of Mr. Yves Leduc. It happened that this man, this strawman, as he is called, got 1,800 votes by mistake and because of the prevailing confusion, with the result that the official Liberal candidate was beaten by 1,700 votes. Without that strawman whose name was placed before the name of the official Liberal candidate, the latter would undoubtedly have been elected.
This is quite as true of the Conservative candidates as of the Liberal candidates. I shall not pretend to have a monopoly, or rather that the Liberal party has a monopoly on honest people. Certain conditions might happen among the Conservatives as among the Liberals, but we should have at least the benefit of having the candidates names written in alphabetical order, for the party in power as well as for the opposition. If
Canada Elections Act
the organizers of the Liberal, or of the Conservative party want to bring in strawmen, well, the names of those strawmen will at least appear after those who were nominated in good faith and received the support, either of the leader of the opposition or of the leader of the party in power.
In the electoral district of Laurier-just to illustrate the point-well, in Montreal-Laurier, a so-called Rene Levesque, who, by the by was an artist, presented nomination papers and we were not even able to find out where he lived. He was completely unknown. However, it happened, thanks to that section in the provincial legislation, that the name of that famous Rene Levesque appeared on the ballot after the Rene Levesque who was the official opposition candidate. That, however, did not stop the famous mystery man, or the famous non-existent Rene Levesque, from obtaining 900 votes, in spite of the hundreds and hundreds of dollars that were spent to explain to the people that this Rene Levesque was not the candidate of the party which is now in power.
The situation did not occur on the federal level, but in the provincial election.
The object of this amendment-and I am, at least, ready to admit it-is to eliminate strawmen in some electoral districts.
Fictitious candidates were presented by friends or opponents, it is all one to me; but if such non-existent candidates are to be presented, at least their names will be listed after those of the official candidates. In other words, their names will no longer be printed at the best place on the ballot, because I need not tell you, Mr. Chairman, that when people want to be dishonest, as happened recently, they will find a Rene Levesque or some other namesake. Had it not been for the provincial act, a certain Albert Levesque would have been found and his name would have been placed before that of Mr. Rene Levesque, the official candidate of the Liberal party.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to prolong the debate but I should like to make a few remarks about the amendment.
First of all, I must say I disagree with the C.C.F. party leader. I do not think this amendment constitutes an antidemocratic measure, and that it is so unfavourable to the second opposition party. On the contrary, I think this amendment would help avoid confusion in some way, and for that reason, it seems acceptable to me.
In my particular case, it is doubly acceptable because I have precisely experienced the fear of having to face such confusion in the 1958 election. In fact, I was nervous until

Canada Elections Act
the last moment of the nomination, because, on the Liberal side, one Maurice Johnson, so it seems, had been arrayed as candidate. It was known that he existed and I was afraid he would be presented in order to confuse the electors. Fortunately, the Liberals repented just before the nomination, and I did not have to face that difficulty.
About the remarks made by the hon. member for St. Denis, I thought I could note some reference to the last provincial election. If he were a little less partisan, he would mention not only the case of Mr. Rene Levesque, but also that of the candidate in the constituency of Bourget, Mr. McDuff. There was, in that constituency, one Mr. Jean M'eunier who was accused of having promoted the candidacy of one Roland McDuff in order to confuse the electors and to take away votes from the official candidate, Mr. Romeo McDuff.
Consequently, if the hon. member for St. Denis wants to discuss a problem, I would ask him to do so in an impartial way and to quote the facts, both favourable or unfavourable, to his party. It is not that way he will really show his impartiality.

Mr. Chairman, I am under the impression that our C.C.F. friends possibly believe they would be wronged by the amendment that I moved. For this reason, Mr. Chairman, may I ask you to put off the vote on the amendment that I moved.
When the election act was passed in the province of Quebec there were only two parties, while here, in Ottawa, we also have the C.C.F. as well as the Social Credit party. It would therefore be unfair if the names of the official candidates of the C.C.F. and the Social Credit could not be included in the ballot, after those of the Liberal and Conservative party candidates.
If my amendment had been worded in this way, it would have been more regular and fairer for all the parties recognized in the federal parliament. I believe I have made the house understand the reason why I moved this amendment. I had nothing against the Liberals, the Conservatives, the C.C.F. or any other party. I was only thinking of those organizers who, in order to create confusion, find a way to nominate citizens who do not exist at all, or so little, so as to mislead the population and take votes away from those who, normally, would get them.

Mr. Chairman, it is rather surprising that unanimous consent is not given. I should like to illustrate the point. Where you have two identical names you might be able to identify them in some way but I know of a recent occasion when there were three identical names on a ballot. If you do not provide some means of differentiating between the three identical names you can appreciate that a real problem arises for the voter in knowing exactly what to do. This situation has occurred and there is room for confusion. All the amendment seeks to do is to eliminate the confusion.
I think the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville was quite courageous in standing up and supporting the amendment, indicating that he or someone he knows has been a victim of precisely this kind of confusion. I feel that the amendment moved by the hon. member for St. Denis may be somewhat improved in this way. The first thing to appear on the ballot should be a list of all official parties, and the candidates of all official parties. Whether there are two, three or four, they should come first. Following that could appear all the additional names that tend to confuse. I think the amendment should be withdrawn but if hon. members do not give unanimous consent, of course, it cannot be done, and in refusing hon. members are just compounding confusion.

It is a reactionary government and some of the legislation it has introduced is reactionary; there is no doubt about that. In British Columbia the system there is that the designation of the political party to which a candidate belongs appears on the ballot paper along with the name of the candidate. The act also provides that a person cannot run, for example, as an independent Liberal. If there is a Liberal candidate

in a particular riding, and we do have a few in provincial elections, his name would appear along with his party designation. If there is confusion in the ranks of the Liberal party and someone wants to run as an independent Liberal he cannot designate himself as an independent Liberal. He must be an independent, period. He cannot be an independent and attach the name of a political party.
No doubt the hon. member for St. Denis and his colleagues want to find a system to overcome the problem in Quebec that he related, which apparently arises in other places also, but I think they should direct their attention to the placing of the party affiliation on the ballot with the additional proviso that a person must be classified as an independent if he is an independent and not have any party label attached.

Mr. Chairman, until now in the discussion of the C.B.C. estimates, my colleagues have mostly dealt with the cultural point of view. Obviously, two main features must be taken into account when an organization such as the C.B.C. is being considered.
First, there is the matter of ideas. There is also the matter of the technical vehicle to convey those ideas.
As an engineer, I feel it is my duty to point out to my colleagues the technical aspect of the C.B.C.
Canadian engineers, and especially French Canadian engineers, may rightly be proud of the technical achievements of the C.B.C.
If we compare the C.B.C. radio and T.Y. systems with those in other countries, we
Supply-C.B.C.
have no reason to be ashamed of what has been produced in Canada.
Those engineers who performed miracles with so little in so little time, in a vast country with a dual culture, really deserve praise.
We must not forget that Canada had its first radio facilities only a generation ago, that is around 1920, while television began in 1952 and yet more than 96 per cent of Canadian families already have radio coverage and almost 80 per cent enjoy television. We must especially take into account the vastness of our country. In fact, the radio network covers more than 15,000 miles and the T.V. network covers the greater part of the country from sea to sea.
Moreover, we must take into consideration the two cultures existing in this country and I believe that nobody will deny that radio and television are factors which contributed more than anything else to Canadian unity.
We should really take into account the contribution to Canadian unity of that technical means of communication, thanks to the work of our Canadian engineers.
I want to quote a few names: Dr. Augustin Frigon, Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, Lucien L'Allier-now director of the department of the public works of the city of Montreal- Andre Ste. Marie, the present chief engineer, and I unfortunately cannot quote them all, but I believe that all these engineers have a right to our gratitude because of the considerable work they accomplished.
I was able to appreciate, Mr. Speaker, the vast concepts of those technicians who are managing the C.B.C. As technical adviser of the committee on housing and renovation of the city of Montreal, I have been able to satisfy myself of the co-operative mind shown by the representatives of the C.B.C. with regard to the municipal authorities of Montreal, and of their great civic spirit with regard to their French-speaking fellow citizens in the eastern part of central Montreal.
I do not hesitate to pay them tribute publicly for the excellent work they have done in their negotiations with the city of Montreal, in order to find an appropriate site, in Montreal, for the future French language T.V. and radio centre for the whole country.
On behalf of the citizens of the constituency of St. James which I have the honour to represent here, Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the management of the C.B.C. for having had the courage and wisdom to choose

Supply-C.B.C.
as the site of that future T.V. and radio French centre, that old "faubourg de Quebec", in the very heart of the French-speaking population of the centre of the metropolis.
Construction of that huge centre will involve slum clearance and the replacement of those physically and morally filthy houses by comfortable ones. It will increase the value of neighbouring properties, and will bring about shortly the complete renovation of a huge decaying centre, to which no one seemed to pay any interest until now.
I must pay tribute to the vision of Alphonse Ouimet, president of the C.B.C., to his assistant, colonel Rene Landry and to all their associates, who made those negotiations possible and have thus insured the continued technical development of the C.B.C.
I trust Mr. Chairman, that this project which has been approved and supported by the downtown Montreal businessmen's association called the centre commercial de Montreal and by many other business and civic organizations in eastern Montreal will also be approved by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker), for the benefit of the Montreal area, the province of Quebec and the whole of Canada.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Chairman, let me stress once again the technical aspects of the C.B.C. Those aspects should retain a dominant position in a country as large as ours, where communications are of vital importance. It would be unfortunate if the heights reached by our technicians and engineers in the fields of radio and television were forgotten in the midst of quarrels on other aspects of the problem.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am rather flabbergasted at hearing such great truths on the C.B.C. from the mouth of a Conservative member from Quebec, and would ask for leave to call it ten o'clock. Are we sitting till eleven o'clock?

speechtext:
I am not mixed up, you are the ones who will be confused if you listen to my speech.
Mr. Chairman, first I should like to commend the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Campeau) for sounding a very refreshing note, quite different from the others we have

heard on the estimates of the C.B.C., as introduced by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan).
I am greatly interested in the operations of the C.B.C., and I know every Canadian is interested, while the French network is of concern to every French-speaking Canadian, not only in the province of Quebec, but throughout Canada. I believe the former administration as well as the present one have done much to extend in the other provinces the service of the French network to our compatriots. And it is also for that reason that I have been a little concerned by the remarks made in this house by certain Conservative members from Quebec.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul), for one, proffered many charges. But he did not bring any proof of what he said. He complained that the C.B.C. does not encourage local artists, that the corporation brought in from Paris a Canadian songstress to sing Canadian songs. I believe it is time that his colleagues make their choice between what they want and what they do not want; and once they have made their choice, they should work in an intelligent way to reach their goal.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere also criticized an employee of the corporation for having stayed at the Windsor hotel for a certain number of days in February 1959.
If his memory serves him right, he will recall that this was at about the time when we had a strike of the corporation's employees in Montreal. Could it not be, perchance, that the employee who stayed at the Windsor hotel in Montreal was an official of the head office who would have had to move to Montreal for this whole period in order to meet the authorities of the C.B.C., the local authorities and the striker's representatives?
The hon. member then gave a list of programs and mentioned names. I agree with him on certain points. I do not approve of all the programs of the C.B.C. They do not all please me. But, I do not think that my taste should be the standard of the taste of all other Canadians. There are some programs I like and others I do not like.
The hon. member told us how much those programs cost. I would have been much interested to know what kind of programs he would have substituted to those who are already on the C.B.C. schedule. And, once again, I readily agree that the C.B.C. does

not produce perfect programs only. The corporation tries to improve, I hope, and if we consider helping it, it is not only by criticizing those who look after the programming that we shall succeed.
The hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere told us how surprised he was at what happened on the French radio network, on the French T.V. network, the night of June 22nd. He stated, as if he had the proof, that Hon. Dozois, Hon. Thibault, Hon. Bertrand and Hon. Johnson were not invited to appear on television following the June 22nd development in the province of Quebec. I ran twice as a candidate at elections in my region where we have a private T.V. station. I remember very well, and I still have the documents that the local station wrote twice during both elections to invite all the candidates to appear on television to make any comments they wished, whether elected or defeated. And I remember very well answering twice that whatever the results might be, I would go; therefore, I would be very surprised if the C.B.C. which has a wide experience in that field, had not done the same.
I shall certainly inquire of responsible authorities and write to none other than the hon. Minister of National Revenue who will supply me, I hope, with this information.
Those are accusations that are altogether unfounded and vicious. I admit that some C.B.C. people may not be doing their duty. Some people in the C.B.C. have faults like anybody in this house. There are in the province of Quebec certain people who sincerely want to help those persons who have built our French television network. If these people wish to make an intelligent contribution, it is not by throwing mud at people in parliament, that they will succeed. If these people are intelligent, and I am sure that many of them are, they are going to inquire and if they should come up with facts showing that this or that happened, and should they really want to help the minister and the authorities of C.B.C. they will acquaint the latter of their findings and ask them to act. If the minister does not do anything, I would then understand, in those circumstances, that the hon. members would want to rise in the house to unburden their mind, referring then to the famous mopping-up at C.B.C.

Yet, he should know that the C.B.C. has earned several trophies. Again last year, if my memory serves me right, it earned the Italia trophy in an international competition, for its interpretation of dramatical works. As I just said, the trophies earned by the C.B.C. are innumerable; but it is certainly no thanks to the recommendation of certain Conservative members from Quebec that it has been able to earn those international trophies.
If we want to be genuinely sincere in the purposes we want to achieve, in the speeches

we make in this house, I think we should be in a position to prove our statements. I repeat what I said a moment ago: if we really want to help the Minister of National Revenue to fulfil his functions in an efficient, practical and concrete way, let us go and see him in his office, let us give him proof of what we claim, let us tell him our concern about the improvement of the management of the C.B.C. and of its programs. Let us offer our cooperation to the minister. But let us not come here in the house to be the laughingstock of our colleagues from the nine other provinces.
I resent that way of doing things, because, like several other members, I am not that kind of Canadian. In behaving that way, Mr. Chairman, we are opening doors to the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) who is always too happy to use them.
Through this kind of behaviour, we also justify the first sentence of the speech delivered in this house by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) on the C.B.C. estimates. Unfortunately, I do not have the text of his speech at hand, but I think I recall that the hon. member said something like this:
"Mr. Chairman, when those quarrels are over in Quebec, I shall commence."
I should like to revert, for the last time, to what I was saying a moment ago. It is the responsibility of any hon. member who has something serious against the C.B.C. to call on the proper authorities and place the evidence on their desk and say: "Unless you do something about it, we will arouse public opinion". Ministers or authorities should not be subjected to blackmail. The proper way is to call on them and tell them candidly what is wrong, with appropriate proof, and then to say: "Now it is your duty to act". And if they refuse to act, then there is ample time to do what has been done in this house since

Mr. Chairman, such tactics are such as to arouse suspicions in every citizen not only of the province of Quebec, but of other provinces as well, as to the things going on in our province.
Mr. Chairman, I intend to check a few of the accidental and unfounded charges made in this house, and I will certainly speak plainly when the occasion arises.
Apparently, an attempt is being made to use the tactics of Voltaire, who would often say: "Keep lying and lying, and eventually

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word to the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin). Should a person who gets a dustpan and a broom to pick up what has been thrown on the floor be insulted? That is what I am trying to do presently, and my honourable friends from the province of Quebec are shocked. The proper course to follow would have been not to throw anything on the floor and to act like responsible men in this house.
Mr. Chairman, I take pleasure in telling the house that the Conservative members from Quebec are not all of that stamp, and I am glad of that, for one would get a wrong idea of the province of Quebec if I were to say they are all alike. One must not see it through certain speeches on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that were made in this house.
The French network of the C.B.C. is not free of all mistakes, as I have said, and many others too, but if we compare it to the television service in France, I feel that our network is doing very well. In fact, it has taken away many international trophies from the television network of France. And yet France has a population of little over 44 million inhabitants. Its television system operates 50 to 53 or 54 hours a week.
We in Canada have a little more than 18 million people. Our French network can reach 5 million listeners or viewers and is on the air for 75 hours a week.
As I said, there is not a single year when C.B.C. does not win a great number of trophies for its radio and television programs. As recently as last year, the C.B.C. won the prize for good citizenship which was awarded to it by the United States National Safety Council, at Columbus, Ohio. It has been the same in many other fields.
That does not mean that all C.B.C. programs have a very high quality. It does not mean either that everything that is broadcast over the same network is likely to satisfy the most voracious intellectual appetites in my province.
But we must take into consideration a certain balance in the programming of the C.B.C.
Supply-C.B.C.
That is the tough part. I am not saying that the C.B.C. is successful in maintaining that certain balance. I am saying that it is difficult for the authorities of the corporation to develop that balance and to succeed in maintaining it.
However, if we want to help the corporation, we can convey our ideas to it and discuss the matter with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). There is nothing he would like better than a sound administration of the C.B.C. Nothing he would like better than to see the corporation broadcasting programs in accordance with the taste of the majority of the viewers and listeners.
I would like also, Mr. Chairman, to say a word about the international service of the C.B.C. Everyone recalls that this international service was set up during the last world war.
I do not think I would exaggerate the role that it played and is still playing by saying that it projects a picture of Canada in the various countries where it is heard.
I do not think I would err either in saying that the international service of the C.B.C. spreads the ideals of our democracy, of our way of life and that of the western countries.
I must admit quite frankly that the former administration, particularly in the latter years-it was at the time of the Liberal government, and this time will come back soon- did not always fully understand the part the international service plays. But the present administration does not understand it either. At the time of its creation, we realized the psychological influence it could have on the countries where it broadcast its programs.
As for Russia, that country fully realizes the whole influence of the international service that it established. Russia realizes it to the extent that it started three or four months ago, I believe, a daily service to Africa.
The publicity machinery, propagandist of Soviet Russia, is fantastic. It is nothing new for anybody to say that Russia will soon open a university that will be called the international friendship university. This institution will extend free admission to students from Latin America, Asia and Africa.
Those students will be treated in such a way that they will never forget, once they are back home, the kindness shown to them.
In brief, Russia leaves no stone unturned to make known its ambitions, its philosophy, its way of thinking, its Leninism or its Khrushchevism.

Supply-C.B.C.
It seems to me that in Canada, within the limits of our financial possibilities evidently, we should contribute more to the propagating of the ideals of our democratic system.
Consequently, I urge the Minister of National Revenue to try to get a better understanding of the significance for us and for our spiritual and intellectual values, of the work done abroad, and often in countries behind the iron curtain, by the international service in all fields.
The director of the international service- I am talking from experience, because without ever being in charge of that service I worked there for two years-the director is working under difficult conditions. Concerning the programming of political or politically related programs abroad, the director of the international service must keep in constant touch with the authorities of the Department of External Affairs.
Furthermore, he maintains a close contact with the Minister of National Revenue, the treasury board and the national network. Thus, this director has to deal with a lot of employers.
I believe, it is at least my impression, on seeing the budget being cut down each year, that he has to begin, anew, each time he meets an employer, to explain the importance of the international service.
I would like to see the present government give consideration to this matter and make it less difficult and less arduous for the director of the international service to operate.
Once again, Mr. Chairman, I wish to remember how things were when I was myself an employee of the corporation in that department.
I have not seen the director of the international service for months. I say that for the benefit of my hon. friends who are always ready to say that we meet with the authorities in order to get information. I do not think they do us any harm in that respect.
Last year, in fact in this house, an hon. member produced a copy of a brief which could not have been obtained without the collusion of a C.B.C. employee. This copy of the brief was certainly not obtained through the help of a member of the Liberal party.
In brief, Mr. Chairman, I believe that the C.B.C. French network has made a very great contribution-and I want to be fair to

the hon. member for Berthier-Maski-nonge-Delanaudiere who said so in his remarks, the contribution made by the French network to Canada's national unity has been very substantial. The present government also did its best in this regard.
I should like all of us to understand that we must keep our French network, and that if we want to improve it we ought not to behave as we have been behaving right here in the face of our people.
I urge my fellow members from the province of Quebec to consider this thought. If they really want to help the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, let them make representations to persons in authority.
Their government is in power, and their government is therefore able to help the C.B.C. Let the minister be approached and hear the complaints, and I am sure he will be responsible enough to take the necessary steps, when he has evidence.
In concluding, I want to tender my deepest sympathy to the Minister of National Revenue with regard to certain accusations voiced against him, in a very veiled and clever way, by some hon. members in this house. If I might repeat a suggestion I already made, I would say that he might appoint as chairman of that corporation, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay), who has great qualifications. Moreover, he might give him as assistant the hon. member for Chambly-Rou-ville, and as judicial authority who would investigate it all and superintend the latter's work, well, Mr. Chairman, he might appoint the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-De-lanaudiere (Mr. Paul).
I hope the minister will take-

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have
listened with much pleasure and amusement to the speech which has just been delivered in this house. I think the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, in the full sense of the word, has had a good idea in recalling the memory of Voltaire and of his famous saying:
Lie and keep lying; some of it is bound to stick.
He could not have said better, under the circumstances, to describe his party and his own words.
Mr. Speaker, of his entire speech, what I remember is the courage and boldness which he has shown when he said with feeling: "I shall try to summarize my thought." In fact, much courage and boldness were necessary, but I would say the only things lacking were competence and subject matter.

maintopic: REPORTED BAN ON FAREWELLS TO CREWS OF NORTHERN SUPPLY SHIPS
speechtext: You have it all.

maintopic: REPORTED BAN ON FAREWELLS TO CREWS OF NORTHERN SUPPLY SHIPS
speechtext:
What I must emphasize also is the gracious nomination he kindly made. He kindly recommended that I become through Her Majesty's gracious intervention, the president of the C.B.C. Please note-and I dare admit it-that I would be glad of it, were it not that I really have no such pretension. All the criticisms I have made in this house had only one purpose, Mr. Chairman, and it was to reply to the representations, criticisms, questions and requests addressed to me by my electors, by those who have asked me legitimately to represent them here, and by all those who, in the province of Quebec, are concerned, and rightly so, about the atmosphere which exists particularly on the French network of the C.B.C.
I heard a moment ago my hon. colleague declare bluntly that we had indulged in mud slinging, that we had thrown garbage on the floor of this house, and that he had given himself the mission of picking it up. I regret, Mr. Chairman, but I will not be so insolent as to believe that my colleague is a garbage collector, but none the less I should like to denounce that cheap accusation he has made. I thought he was intelligent, I still believe it, except that, after what he said tonight, I am unable to award him the good points I would have liked to give the excellent student he seemed to be when we were in school together.
79951-0-389
Supply-C.B.C.
I do not wish to come back tonight on the subjects I have already dealt with many times. On several occasions, I looked into the problems of the C.B.C., especially those of the French network. I have always been careful to note that the C.B.C. had rendered outstanding services to our country. And if my hon. colleague wishes to refer to the first speech I delivered in this house about the C.B.C., he will be able to read on page 4264 of the French version of Hansard what I said then and which is far removed from the words he dared put in my mouth. This is what I said:
It Is appropriate, I think, to commend the promoters of that movement. They tried in complete good faith to protect us from being too much affected by the United States civilization. At the same time, they have set up a state-owned organization whose value we shall never praise too much.
I repeated the same praises time and again and particularly a few months ago. This is what I said, and this can be found in Hansard of April 8, 1960,-I cannot give the exact page because I have here a separate copy,-
I shall have the opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to come back to the specific matter of programs. I shall then be able to specify the general criticisms I have just made, because it is not my intention to cast reflection on those C.B.C. officials who are doing remarkable work with a scrupulous conscientiousness and in a spirit steeped in the best cultural traditions.
There again, Mr. Chairman, I had praised with much good faith, and also with much pleasure the excellent productions of the C.B.C. No one will deny that the French network, in particular-it is the one I am especially interested in-has given us excellent productions and put excellent programs on the air, but this does not prevent me from criticizing the corporation and denouncing the abuse which creeps in its activities.
The hon. member who spoke before me said that we were making against the C.B.C. a case which consisted in unsubstantiated denunciations, in unfounded charges. I, myself, pointed out on various occasions that the C.B.C. has a well known sympathy for certain people representing a certain school of thought. I pointed out, that most of the time the forum programs had commentators who are invited so often that they seem to be life pensioners of the corporation.
I would like to give here an example of a case in which I have been, not the victim, but the object. In October 1959, that is-if I may use legal terms-on or about

Supply-C.B.C.
October 23, 1959, I received from Montreal a phone call from a moderator or rather-I beg your pardon-the producer of the program "Tribune libre", who invited me to participate in a panel program whose theme was to be the following: "Is a member of parliament free within his own party?" The person who called me gave me many details and I asked him the following question: "Who will be invited on this program?" He replied: "Well, sir, we are trying to have a balance of opinions. That is why we invited representatives of the various political parties, that is a representative of the Liberal party, one of the Conservative party, and one from the Rassemblement des Electeurs, a party which does not exist outside the province of Quebec. That is what I was told by the person who called me. I was also told there would be an independent member. When I asked for details, I was told that Pierre Elliot-Trudeau would represent the Rassemblement, that Paul Lacoste would be the moderator; that the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) would represent the Liberal party, despite his Conservative background; and I was told that the independent member would of all people, be the former Liberal member for Quebec-Montmorency, Mr. Wilfrid Lacroix. I then asked the caller: Are you kidding, or are you being serious? He said Mr. Lacroix had always been an independent member, and there the matter rested. I refused, on the following grounds: I felt that in that particular instance, the C.B.C. was obviously displaying a partisan attitude in inviting on the same panel two representatives of the Liberal party. That is what prevented me from taking part in this program "Tribune Libre".
I could mention many other cases of this type, Mr. Chairman, but the speeches I have made so far on the subject of the C.B.C. have dealt mainly with the attitude and mood prevailing in the C.B.C. Last year, I stated my position quite clearly. I denounced certain attitudes, and at no time would I hesitate to repeat what I said, because as a citizen and a representative of several thousands of citizens, I have a right to say quite candidly what I sincerely believe about the C.B.C. But I did more than denounce attitudes; or accuse individuals, I made suggestions. I was quite surprised that a moment ago, the hon. member who spoke before me made no mention of them. I would simply refer him to the speech I made last Friday, in which I

made suggestions, notably for setting up a royal commission on the administration of the C.B.C.
A commission whose main purpose would not be to inquire only into broadcasting in general, as was the case especially for the Fowler commission, but a commission which would examine in detail all the aspects of the C.B.C. administration.
And I repeat, not with a view to uncovering scandals, to accusing this one or that one, but with a view to giving the people the satisfaction of knowing how the C.B.C. uses the taxpayers money. Such a request has been made for years and we have yet to receive a satisfactory answer. We were told the other day, I think it was, by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets): "But you only have to ask questions." Mr. Chairman, I feel that it is unfair to say "put your questions to the officials and the minister sitting in front of you". Last year, we had a parliamentary committee. We put the questions we were urged by the public to put and we did not get any answers. We were laughed at and got vague and often insolent replies. I, myself have been treated in such an overbearing manner by highly placed officials in the C.B.C. And when I asked, for instance, what principles and criteria were followed by the corporation in such and such a case and for such and such a program, I was told that the aim of the corporation was to present wholesome and entertaining programs. That was not the answer I was looking for. I wanted to know what was the governing idea, the line of thought of those in charge of the C.B.C., and especially of programming, and if their aim was to present programs in accordance to French thought and French culture and to religious and moral principles from which we seek inspiration.
Mr. Chairman, allow me before I conclude to clear up a matter. I usually ignore the stupid remarks that the member for Hull (Mr. Caron) takes the liberty of uttering in this house. However, for the sake of truth I must challenge the insanities he uttered the other day, especially at page 17 of the appendix to Hansard where he said in a language which, with your permission, Mr. Chairman, I shall not qualify:
He should be the last one to complain about patronage-
That is I.
-because, if my memory serves me right- (si je me rappelle bien)

Of course, he should have said "si je me le rappelle bien", because here we are dealing with a transitive verb.
-following a vote, he went to the C.B.C.- and, which is rather unusual-asked to he interviewed during the news broadcast in order to explain his vote in the House of Commons. I do not know of any other member who has been authorized by the C.B.C. to explain a vote he had cast the very same afternoon.
Mr. Chairman, what I am up against, are not the barbarisms and solecisms of the excerpt I just read out, but the absolute lack of truth in what it contains, which in no way describes the real facts. I have never, at any time, asked anybody in the C.B.C. to be interviewed in the news. The statement made by the member for Hull is incorrect and absolutely contrary to the facts.
Mr. Chairman, this evening I would have liked to come back on certain matters which have already been dealt with, but I wonder whether it is really necessary to do so. The suggestions I made the other day clearly indicate my views and my intentions. But in order to satisfy the conscience of the Liberal members who like to hear us asking questions, I shall ask the Minister of National Revenue the following: "What is the policy of the C.B.C. with regard to tenders for any sort of contracts? Are tenders called for buildings, for instance? Are tenders called for the purchase of materials entering, for instance, into settings and costumes? Are tenders called for each of those items?" The question was asked last year, and no satisfactory answer has yet been given.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I should like, in closing my remarks, to thank the C.B.C. for the magnificent productions it has given in the past. I do not hesitate to do it tonight, as every time I took the floor in this house.
And I should like also to call the attention of my colleagues on the fact that our purpose, our desire, is not to find quarrel with the senior officials of the corporation, not to indict such and such individual, but that our desire is simply to know how things are done in the C.B.C., how public funds are utilized and how are chosen the various persons responsible for the education of the public, for its entertainment and recreation.
I should like to recall at this point the principles set out in the corporation's white paper on the particular problem of information. I quote:
79951-0-3891
Supply-C.B.C.
1.	The air belongs to the people, who have a right to hear the main points of view on any important question.
2.	The air must not come under the domination of individuals or groups who are powerful because of their resources or particular situation.
3.	The right to rebuttal is inherent in the democratic doctrine of freedom of speech.
4.	Freedom of speech and the free exchange of opinions are two of the main bulwarks of the freedom of institutions.
And I add this in reply to those who say we are wrong in referring to political favoritism in the C.B.C. and to a monopoly in the field of thought. To reply to this, I will quote an excerpt from the address of Mgr. Paul-Emile Gosselin on the influence of the press, motion picture, radio and television during the 34th social week of Canada. I quote from page 180 of the report:
However, we do not believe that the state radio and television wholly and faithfully reflect the national sense of French Canada. The goal is difficult to achieve in such a field. Without engaging in discussions which seem rather useless, we would wish that all the schools of national thought would have access to the official tribunes. To that end, those who are in charge of the programs would have to be broadminded enough to admit that some people may entertain opinions that are different from theirs on free matters and that there are, outside their circles, sincere patriots who are familiar with the problems of the day.

I have a few remarks to make on this subject. The brevity of my remarks, however, should not be construed by the minister or by the C.B.C. to mean that our problem is not a big one. I wish the minister in showing his appreciation for my few brief remarks, would pay special heed to our problem.
Our problem is not a new one. Representations have been made by me in the past and by the hon. member for Churchill, the hon. member for Dauphin and other members from that particular area who are interested in bringing television to that area of northern Manitoba. My interest is this. If television were extended into that area, my riding also would be served. The need is there. I will not go into that phase of it. The sentiments I feel on this subject were expressed by the hon. member for Churchill. I should like only to say that I concur fully with what he has already said.
My correspondence with the president of the C.B.C. led me to believe that if an announcement were to be made of a policy

Supply-C.B.C.
setting out any extension into the north we would be duly informed. However, I note that recently a statement was made to the effect that kinescope recordings will be made available to that area of The Pas and other places. This is better than nothing. However this presents a further problem. Recently the Yorkton station had its services extended into the areas in Manitoba of Swan River and Dauphin. I am sure the people of that area appreciate that fact. However, the further problem is that the area in between Swan River and Dauphin and the areas of The Pas and Flin Flon are unserved. The service is poor at best. As a matter of fact, the chamber of commerce in the town of Hudson Bay suggested that unless the television service would soon be improved they would advertise for an optometrist.
On reviewing the report of the Fowler commission I note that the forecast of net operating expenditures for 1958, 1959 and 1960, in round figures, were $44 million, $50 million and $55 million and that government estimates were $51 million, $58 million and $62 million, again in round figures. It is to be noted there that the government estimates were in most cases higher than the forescast that was made by the Fowler commission, that is, on their net operating expenditures. Again, on the estimates of capital costs, for the same respective years, the Fowler commission forecast $10 million, $14 million and $13 million for the years 1958, 1959 and 1960 respectively, in round figures, and the government estimates were $8 million, $9 million and $7 million for the respective years.
It seems that we have sacrificed expansion because of increased operating costs. I should only like to say that those operating costs are perhaps in some cases warranted. The operating costs fall into one of three categories that I have mentioned, namely requests for second stations, extensions of time so that television can be viewed earlier in the day and requests for coloured television. I submit that this is hardly fair.
An example of the first category, namely requests for second stations, is to be found in the city of Edmonton in connection with the new station there. I will not dwell on that matter. As for the other two points, I wish the minister would enlighten us and indicate whether, where there is an extension of time, this has meant that the operating costs are greater and that we have been sacrificed in that we are not able to get television because of that fact. Again, I say that is not fair.
[Mr. Korchinski.l
The third point is one which will perhaps become more serious. There is no doubt that there will be a certain amount of agitation for colour television. Agitation for colour television could come only from areas at present served. I wish the minister in summing up would assure us that no such consideration will be given unless areas now unserved are given a chance to get at least some television.
